docs.title: Public API and stability policy
docs.text:
Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

This page says what a host may depend on and what may change. It describes the code of the first release, 0.1.0, and of main after it.

All classes live in one Java package, ai.humem.tiervec, and every class that a host needs is public. Some other classes are public only because the classes of the library call each other. This page separates the two groups. The package has the name of the library, and the Maven coordinates are ai.humem:tiervec.

docs.title: Supported classes
docs.text:
The supported surface is these classes, their public members as listed here, and the behavior that PROVIDER-CONTRACT.md marks exists today.

Class What it is Supported members VecIndex The interface of every index All Hit One result: an id and a score, higher is better All Metric COSINE, DOT, L2 All TieredIndex The index a host database uses: exact tail, sealed segments, merges, batches, checkpoint and reopen The constructors, add, delete, search (all overloads), apply, awaitCapacity, filterScanBelow, sealNow, mergeNow, awaitIdle, rebuildFrom (all overloads), epoch, checkpoint, open (all overloads), openFallbackCause, config, stats, segmentSizes, lastError, size, dim, metric, bytesHeld, close TieredIndex.Config, TieredIndex.Stats, TieredIndex.Batch, TieredIndex.IdVector, TieredIndex.Snapshot, TieredIndex.SearchResult, TieredIndex.Freshness The records and the enum of the tier All RecordSource What a host offers so that TieredIndex.open can reconcile persisted state with the host's records All FlatIndex, GraphIndex, IvfIndex Standalone indexes: exact and quantized scan, concurrent HNSW, inverted file The constructors, the methods of VecIndex, the nested Params of GraphIndex and IvfIndex, and the maintenance and diagnostic methods that each class documents in its Javadoc Quant, Sq8Kernel The code kind and the SQ8 kernel that the flat index and the tier configuration name All SegmentFormat.CorruptException, SegmentFormat.UnsupportedException, SegmentFormat.MismatchException What TieredIndex.open throws for damage, for a newer format, and for files of another index definition The three nested classes. The rest of SegmentFormat is internal

Public members of the supported classes that are not in the table are for tests and diagnostics. They can change in any release: TieredIndex.setSealHooks, activity, workerAlive, segmentCount, pendingTail, sealRatePerSec and setSealRatePerSec; GraphIndex.seal and GraphIndex.fromSealed, which use the internal type SealedGraph.

The maintenance and diagnostic methods of the standalone indexes (for example IvfIndex.listSkew, FlatIndex.slotsUsed) are supported, but the three standalone indexes are the least settled part of the surface. A change to one of them is listed in the changelog like any other.

docs.title: Internal classes
docs.text:
These classes are public but not supported. They carry the annotation @Internal. A host must not use them. They can change or disappear in any release, with no changelog line.

Class What it is FaultHook A seam for tests that stops a publish after a step Manifest The manifest file of a checkpoint SealedGraph An immutable graph segment, in memory and as a file SegmentFormat The constants and helpers of the segment file (except the three exception classes above) SegmentInfo The facts that a segment file header holds SegmentReader Reads a segment file SegmentWriter Writes a segment file

The test ApiSurfaceTest checks this page against the code: every public top-level class is either in the supported table or marked @Internal, and the two lists here match the annotation. All other classes of the package are package-private.

A module descriptor that exports only the supported classes is not possible while the internal classes share the package with them. Moving them to a separate package would be a later, breaking change.

docs.title: Stability policy for 0.x
docs.text:
The version is 0.MINOR.PATCH until the API is stable (see the plan in issue 61).

  • A breaking change to the supported surface needs a new minor version, and a line in CHANGELOG.md that says what to change.
  • A patch release never makes a breaking change to the supported surface.
  • Breaking means: a supported class or member is removed, renamed or moved; a signature, a return type or a thrown checked exception changes; a record gets a new component (its constructor changes, unless the old constructor stays, as TieredIndex.Config does for its earlier form); or behavior changes against a guarantee that PROVIDER-CONTRACT.md marks exists today.
  • Not breaking: a new class, a new method, a new overload, or a new constant in an enum. An added enum constant is listed in the changelog.
  • A guarantee marked partly or planned in the contract can change in any minor release.
  • The internal classes and the members that are not in the table above can change in any release.
  • The file format has its own version. Read SEGMENT-FORMAT.md for what a reader accepts. A change to the format that an older reader refuses is listed in the changelog.
  • At 1.0 the rule tightens: a breaking change then needs a new major version.

The Javadoc of the supported classes says what each method does, and it is the reference for the details.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

The harness is src/bench/java/ai/humem/tiervec/Bench.java. It builds a TieredIndex from seeded data, compares every answer with an exact scan that it computes itself, and writes one result file that names the machine, the JDK and the commit. It measures one question set: recall and latency of the tier at a size, unfiltered and filtered, and what happens when writers and searchers run at once. Issue #12 (the range of allowed shares where an exact scan beats the graph walk) is the first user.

Numbers from the harness are directional unless a study states its claim, its arms, its number of runs and its bound before it runs (see "How to read measurements" in ROADMAP.md). One run is one sample. A result file says what the run did on one machine, not what the library does on every machine.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Maven does not compile the harness, as with src/smoke. Compile it with the library sources, and run it with the Vector API module (the module is optional for the library, but a result without it is a different measurement, and the file records which one ran):

mkdir -p target/bench/classes
find src/main/java src/bench/java -name '*.java' > target/bench/sources.txt
javac -d target/bench/classes --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector @target/bench/sources.txt
java -Xmx14g --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector -cp target/bench/classes ai.humem.tiervec.Bench \
  --host-label my-laptop --out results/$(date +%F)-my-laptop.txt

With no options this is the 1,000,000-vector run: dimension 768, cosine, k = 10, ef = 100, 200 queries with 5 timed passes, allowed shares 0.5, 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001 each with filterScanBelow off and on, then 10 minutes of concurrent writers and searchers. Every option is a --key value pair, and the list with the defaults is the method Bench.defaults(). The ones that matter most:

Option Default Meaning --n, --dim, --k, --ef 1000000, 768, 10, 100 Vectors, dimension, answers per query, beam width of a segment search --seed 42 Seed of the data, the queries and the filter. The same seed gives the same vectors on every JVM (the DATA line has a checksum) --ef-sweep 20,50,200,400 Extra unfiltered cells at these beam widths, a recall curve like the one of GraphTest bench. The recall floors do not apply to them --queries, --reps 200, 5 Distinct queries, and timed passes over them per cell (after one warm-up pass that also measures recall) --shares 0.5,0.1,0.01,0.001 Allowed shares of the filtered cells --scan-below 0,1 filterScanBelow values of the filtered cells. 0 is off (the walk, with its fallback to a scan). 1 scans first at every share --tail-limit, --small-limit, --max-segments, --merge-fan, --build-threads the library defaults The tier configuration. --build-threads 0 keeps the default of TieredIndex.Config --load add add calls TieredIndex.add n times and waits until no seal or merge is due. rebuild makes one rebuildFrom --settle none merge calls mergeNow() after the build, so the searches run on one segment --conc-seconds 600 Length of the concurrent phase. 0 skips it --writers, --searchers 2, 2 Threads of the concurrent phase. There is one more thread that deletes --write-rate, --delete-rate 500, 100 Adds and deletes per second over all threads. 0 for adds is unthrottled --min-recall, --min-scan-recall 0, 0 Recall floors. With 0 the harness reports and does not fail on recall. The CI smoke sets both --host-label the host name The name of the machine in the file. The file is meant to be committed to a public repository, so give a label that says what the machine is and not who owns it --out none The result file. The same lines go to standard output

The exit code is 0 when every check passed, 1 when a check failed (see "Checks" below), and 2 for a wrong option.

Memory, as an estimate that no run has confirmed yet: the harness holds the vectors (n times dimension times 4 bytes, 3.1 GB at the default), the tier holds its own copy of every vector, and a merge builds a new segment while it still holds the old ones. Allow about 10 GB of heap at 1,000,000 vectors of dimension 768 and give the JVM -Xmx14g. The MEMORY lines of a result file give what the run used.

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
• Vectors. A Gaussian mixture on the unit sphere: --clusters (100) unit centroids drawn from the seed, and the vector of an id is normalize(centroid + sigma * noise) with --sigma 0.4 (the generator GraphT.Gen of the tests, which GraphTest bench also uses). The cluster of an id and the noise are a function of the seed and the id only, and the Gaussian uses StrictMath, so the data does not depend on the machine.
  • Queries. --queries vectors of the same distribution, with ids that are not in the index (from 2^50 up). They are not inserted.
  • Filter. An id is allowed when a hash of the id and the seed, as a number in [0, 1), is below the share. The allowed sets of the shares are nested (the set of 0.01 is inside the set of 0.1), and the filter does not depend on the vector. A filter that is correlated with the vectors, such as one tenant per cluster, behaves differently and is not measured here.
  • Metric. Cosine. The vectors have unit length, so the exact scan uses the dot product.

docs.title: The exact scan and recall
docs.text:
The harness computes the exact top k of every query with its own scalar dot product, in one pass over the vectors on all available cores. It does not use a kernel of the library, so a wrong kernel cannot hide behind itself. It does that for the unfiltered query and for every share. Recall@k of a query is the share of the exact ids that the answer contains (the truth is the allowed set when the query has a filter). The SEARCH line has the mean over the queries and the minimum. A tie at the boundary of the top k can swap one id, so recall of exactly 1 is not expected from an exact path: the score of an answer is compared with the exact score instead (maxScoreError).

The first pass over the queries in a cell is the warm-up and measures recall. The next --reps passes are timed, one search at a time on one thread, and give p50, p99, p99.9, mean, maximum and operations per second. A cell with scanFirst=true runs the exact scan of the allowed ids in every segment (the plan of DESIGN.md).

docs.title: The result file
docs.text:
One run writes one file, results/<date>-<host-label>.txt, in lines of key=value pairs that start with a tag. It is plain text so that grep reads it. Nothing is written twice: a line is final when it is printed, and a file that does not end with BENCH-END is a run that did not finish.

Tag What it holds BENCH-RESULT, RUN The format number, the start time and the host label COMMIT git rev-parse HEAD of the repository at run time, and the number of modified tracked files (0 for a clean tree) SEED The seed and the data model CPU, CPUFLAGS, CPUFREQ, RAM The model of the first allowed core and its flags (a hybrid CPU has cores with different flags, so a run pinned to some cores names those), the cores the process may use, the frequency governor, the memory OS, JDK, JVM, VECTORAPI The operating system, the JDK version and vendor, the JVM arguments, the garbage collectors, and whether the Vector API module and the vector kernels were in use PARAMS, CONFIG Every option, and the tier configuration DATA, TRUTH Time to generate the data and to compute the exact answers, a checksum of the first vectors, and the smallest exact answer of each group BUILD, BUILD-STATS, BUILD-T Seconds to add and until the tier was settled, inserts per second, the tier statistics (seals, merges, segment sizes, write amplification, back pressure), and a progress line each minute MEMORY Heap in use and resident memory after a garbage collection, and the peak resident memory SEARCH One cell: kind, share, filterScanBelow, recall, latency percentiles, operations per second, malformed answers, garbage collections during the cell CONC, CONC-T, CONC-WINDOW The concurrent phase: adds, deletes and searches per second, search latency overall and per window, every error, a progress line per window CONC-SETTLE, CONC-CHECK, CONC-RECALL The end state: the live count against the expected count, lastError, and recall against an exact scan of the live set BENCH-SUMMARY, BENCH-FAILURE, BENCH-END OK or FAIL, the list of failed checks, and the end marker

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
The run fails (exit code 1) when:

  • an exception reaches the harness or a thread of the concurrent phase;
  • the live count after the build or after the concurrent phase is not the number of vectors that were added and not deleted (a lost or a phantom vector), or lastError() is set;
  • an answer has more than k hits, scores out of order, an id twice, an id outside the data, or an id that the filter does not allow;
  • a search that began after a delete had returned still finds that id (the deleter deletes the ids 0, 1, 2, ... in order, so the searchers know which deletes were done);
  • a recall floor was set (--min-recall, --min-scan-recall) and a cell is below it.

docs.title: Rules for a run that is meant to be read
docs.text:
1. Pin the process to cores of one kind and run nothing else beside it. Write down the cores: the file records cpusAllowedList. A laptop on battery, with a turbo that varies, or with its low-power cores, is a directional measurement.
  2. Use a JDK that CI tests (Temurin 21 or 25), name it in the file (JDK), and keep the Vector API module on, unless the run is the scalar one on purpose (-Dai.humem.tiervec.scalar=true).
  3. A claim needs the runs that ROADMAP.md asks for, each in a fresh JVM, and a bound that was written down before the first run. One run is a description.
  4. Commit the file with its commit SHA inside, in results/, and say in the table row of the README what it covers.
  5. Do not compare files from different machines or different JDK builds as if only the library changed.

docs.title: The CI smoke
docs.text:
The job bench smoke (JDK 21) and (JDK 25) compiles the harness with the library and runs it at n = 10,000 and dimension 768, with 100 queries, one extra beam width (32), shares 0.1 and 0.01, and 15 seconds of the concurrent phase. It is not a required check, and it runs beside the fast tests. It proves that the harness runs, that its answers agree with its own exact scan, and that the checks above hold on a small tier. It prints timings and has no speed bar: the runner is shared, so a timing is only a ratio inside one run.

The recall floors of the smoke are 0.90 for the unfiltered and the walk cells and 0.99 for the cells that scan first. In the first runs (CI run 43133522549, JDK 21 and 25) recall was 1.0000 unfiltered, 0.997 to 1.0000 for the filtered walk and 1.0000 for every scan-first cell, and a run took 21 to 23 seconds (the job about 30 seconds). The floors leave room for a different structure of the segments from one run to the next, and they are far above what a broken index gives: a tier that returned only its tail would find at most the 20 percent of the data that the tail holds, and the scan-first path is exact apart from a swapped tie at the boundary of the top k. A control step of the job runs the harness with a floor that cannot be met (recall of at least 1.5) and requires exit code 1 and a BENCH-FAILURE line, so the failure path is not a path that never runs.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

This page describes what the code in src/main/java/ai/humem/tiervec does today. It is written from the sources and their Javadoc. Where something is not built yet, it says so.

docs.title: The contract: VecIndex
docs.text:
Every index implements VecIndex, over float[] vectors with a long id and one of three metrics (COSINE, DOT, L2).

  • add, delete and search may be called concurrently from many threads, and a search never throws because of a concurrent write.
  • Read-your-writes: after add(id, v) returns, a search that starts later in any thread can return id. After delete(id) returns, a search that starts later never returns id.
  • Ids are unique: adding an existing id replaces its vector.
  • Hit.score is a similarity and higher is better for every metric (cosine and dot as they are, L2 as the negative squared distance).
  • search(q, k, allow) takes an optional LongPredicate filter and may return fewer than k hits only when fewer than k live vectors qualify.

docs.title: The parts
docs.text: Class What it is FlatIndex Exact or quantized scan over every live vector. No graph. Has serialize and load. GraphIndex Mutable, concurrent HNSW-style graph. seal() turns it into a SealedGraph, fromSealed turns it back. SealedGraph Immutable compact graph. The only mutation is a soft delete through a bitset. Has serialize and load (one segment file, see SEGMENT-FORMAT.md). IvfIndex Standalone inverted-file index with k-means lists and a background retrain. Not a segment type of TieredIndex. TieredIndex The tier: an exact tail in front of sealed graph segments. A settled tier can be written with checkpoint and read with open. Kernels, VKernels, NKernels, Kern, VKern Distance kernels. Kernels picks vector or scalar code once per JVM or image, for the flat, IVF, and graph kernels. NKernels holds the Vector API kernels for a native image: the fp32 dot and squared L2, the int8 dot, the SQ8 dots, and block16; its 128-bit forms of the last four are also what an aarch64 JVM uses for them.

docs.title: Flat index
docs.text:
Vectors live in chunks (the first chunks grow from 64 to 4096 slots, then 4096 per chunk), each with a float array, an id array, a live bitmap, and optional quantized codes. A slot is written once and never reused, so a reader never sees a half-written slot. Appends never copy old data.

The read path takes no lock. A writer fills a slot and then sets its live bit with release semantics, which publishes it. Delete clears the bit. Replace writes a new slot, sets it live, and clears the old bit, so a search can briefly see both copies and the result is de-duplicated by id. Writers take one of 64 stripe monitors by id hash. compact() takes an exclusive lock that pauses writers, never searches.

Quantization is chosen per index:

  • NONE: fp32 scan. The result equals brute force, with ties broken by the smaller id.
  • SQ8: symmetric int8 with one scale per vector. No training, so churn cannot make it stale.
  • BINARY: one sign bit per dimension against a per-dimension threshold, frozen after the first calibration set of live vectors. Until then searches are exact.

A quantized search scans the codes, keeps the best rerankFactor * k candidates, rescores them in fp32, and returns the best k. Returned scores are always exact fp32 scores.

docs.title: Graph index
docs.text:
A multi-layer HNSW graph, with the alpha robust prune of DiskANN (Vamana) as a parameter (alpha = 1 is the HNSW neighbor heuristic). Nodes live in fixed-size chunks and never move. Neighbor lists are copy-on-write arrays published with release and acquire VarHandle stores, so readers take no lock and always see a complete list. Writers take a striped monitor of the owning node, one at a time.

  • add publishes the node's own links, then marks it live, then adds the reverse links, then updates the entry point. A node is returnable only when live, and reachable only through published links.
  • delete marks a node deleted at once. Deleted nodes are still traversed. consolidate() repairs the neighbor lists that hold a tombstone, waits (never blocking a reader) until searches that started earlier are done, and then recycles the slots.
  • A replace is a new node plus a tombstone of the old one.
  • Search is a beam search at layer 0 with a greedy descent above. Filtered-out and deleted nodes are traversed but not collected. With a filter, after a visit budget with fewer than k collected, the search falls back to an exact scan over the nodes that pass the filter.
  • filterScanBelow(fraction) (default 0, off) lets a filtered search skip the walk when the allowed share is small. The share is estimated from 256 id slots spread over the index (a fixed number of predicate calls, no size hint from the host). When at most fraction of the sampled live slots pass, the search scans the allowed ids exactly, which costs one predicate call per live id and returns the exact top k. Above the threshold the search is unchanged. With the option off, a filtered search spends its whole visit budget before the scan when the allowed share is below about ef divided by the budget, and that wasted walk is most of the cost of a filtered search at a share near 0.01 (see issues 12 and 56).
  • With Params.sq8 the traversal uses int8 codes and the final candidates are rescored in fp32. Construction always uses fp32.

docs.title: IVF index
docs.text:
K-means centroids, one append-only list per centroid, and a search probes the nearest nprobe lists. Until the live count reaches trainAt, every search is an exact scan. Training is lazy. needsRetrain() measures drift, list skew, and growth, and retrain() rebuilds the model off to the side while writers continue (their changes go to a log that is replayed), then swaps the new model in with one volatile write. Searches never wait for a retrain. Deletes are tombstones in the lists, and compact() rewrites a list from its live slots.

IVF has no serialization yet, and it is not used by TieredIndex.

docs.title: The tier
docs.text: TieredIndex is the composition. The vectors in the host's records are the source of truth. The tail, the segments, and the floor map are derived data that can be thrown away and rebuilt (rebuildFrom) from raw vectors, so the code never has to make the derived state durable. rebuildFrom swaps the rebuilt state in the way a merge does: a search that started before the swap keeps the floor entries that its segments need, and they are dropped when that search is done.

docs.title: Exact tail
docs.text: add puts the vector into the active tail, a FlatIndex (fp32 or SQ8), and a raw copy next to it. The raw copy is what a seal and a rebuild read. The vector is visible to the next search in any thread before add returns. delete removes it from the tails and hides every segment copy at once. apply does both for a whole batch (see Batches).

docs.title: Sealed HNSW segments
docs.text:
When the active tail reaches tailLimit vectors, or its first vector is older than tailAgeMs, and the index holds at least smallLimit vectors, one worker thread seals it:

  1. Freeze the tail under the write lock. A new empty tail takes over writes.
  2. Build a GraphIndex from the frozen contents and seal it, outside any lock, while searches and writes continue (searches scan both tails).
  3. Publish the segment with one volatile write of an immutable view that drops the frozen tail.

A vector is always in the frozen tail, in the segment, or in both for an instant, and the dedupe resolves the overlap, so it is never missing. Below smallLimit live vectors no graph is built at all and every search is an exact scan.

docs.title: Atomic swap of the segment list
docs.text: The segment list, the active tail, and the frozen tail live in one immutable view. A seal or a merge builds its result off to the side and publishes a new view with a single volatile write. A search reads the view once and finishes on it, so a search that started before a swap still sees everything it needs and the old segments stay valid for it. To keep that true for hidden copies, each view counts the searches running on it: a search raises the count, reads the view again to check that it is still current, and lowers the count when it is done (one atomic add each way, no lock). A view that a swap replaces while its count is not zero is held until the count reaches zero.

docs.title: Batches
docs.text:
apply(batch) is the write path of a host transaction: the adds, then the deletes, under one hold of the write lock. The tail and the floor map change in place, so a new view cannot make a batch visible at one instant. A batch counter does: it is odd while a batch is applied and even otherwise, and only the writer that holds the lock changes it. A search reads it before it scans and waits while it is odd. After the scan it reads it again, behind an acquire fence. When the value changed, a batch was applied during the scan, the answer may mix the state before the batch with the state after it, and the search runs again on the current view. A search that returns therefore saw no batch in progress from the start of its scan to its end: all of every earlier batch and nothing of any later one. A single add or delete does not touch the counter, because each is atomic by itself.

A search that is in the middle of a scan when a batch opens finishes the scan on the view it holds, which is still valid memory, and discards the answer. A search that starts inside the batch waits for it. A search that starts after the batch sees all of it, because the closing write of the counter comes after every change of the batch.

The query path pays one volatile read before the scan and one fence and one volatile read after it, plus a second scan when a batch overlapped the first. A search that meets a batch waits for the length of the batch (a short spin, then parks of 20 microseconds). A stream of batches that follow each other faster than one scan takes can starve a search, so the rate of apply calls is the bound.

docs.title: Tombstones and the version floor
docs.text: Versions come from one counter under the write lock. The floor map says "a segment copy of id is valid only when its version is at least floor[id]". Replace and delete raise the floor, but only when a segment or the frozen tail holds a copy of the id, so the map stays small. Searches filter segments through the floor inside the beam, so a deleted or replaced vector never appears and nothing waits for a merge. Each segment counts its hidden copies, and a segment with none is searched with the plain filter. Because the floor is a version and not a flag, an id that the host reuses after a delete is added with a newer version, so the new vector is visible while the old copies stay hidden.

docs.title: Search
docs.text: A search scans the tails exactly, searches every segment, drops hidden ids, applies the filter in both, and merges by score. Duplicate ids (a replace in flight) are resolved newest source first: active tail, frozen tail, then segments. Freshness.SEALED_ONLY skips the tails. It may lag (a vector added or replaced since the last seal is not in it) but never returns a deleted id, a stale vector, or an id that was never added.

docs.title: Merge
docs.text: When the segment count exceeds maxSegments, or one segment is deadFraction hidden, the worker rebuilds the smallest segments (or the dead one) into one segment from their valid vectors only, throttled to mergeRatePerSec inserts per second so the cores that serve queries are not starved, and swaps it in. Floor entries whose stale copies are gone are dropped at the swap, except those that a segment of a held view still needs: a search that started before the swap can still be scanning an old segment, and without the entry its hidden copy would be valid again. The rest is dropped when the searches of the held views are done: the worker looks again every 5 ms while such a cleanup is pending, and awaitIdle, mergeNow, sealNow and checkpoint finish it on the calling thread, so a tier that awaitIdle reports idle has a settled floor map. The optional size-ratio trigger (mergeTriggerRatio) is described with the knobs.

docs.title: Bounds and threads
docs.text: One worker thread runs one task at a time (a seal or a merge). There is a cap on segments. No allocation proportional to n happens on the query path. Back pressure: when the active tail holds hardTailFactor * max(tailLimit, smallLimit) vectors, add waits for the worker, bounded to 10 s. awaitCapacity(deadline) is the same wait as a pre-check for apply: it waits for room in the tail and returns false at the deadline. apply never waits for the worker and does not look at the limit, so one batch can take the tail above it. add and delete take one write lock for a short time, and apply takes it once for the whole batch. Searches take no lock.

docs.title: Kernels and the scalar twin
docs.text:
Kernels holds the flat-tier distance kernels: float dot and L2, int8 dot, and Hamming. Each has a Vector API version in VKernels and a scalar twin. The choice is made once, when Kernels is initialized: scalar when -Dai.humem.tiervec.scalar=true, scalar when VKernels cannot load (for example without the jdk.incubator.vector module), vector otherwise. Kernels.VECTOR says which one is in use. IvfIndex uses the same kernels.

On a JVM whose preferred float species has fewer than 8 lanes (128 bits: NEON on aarch64), VKernels has no fast form of the int8 dot, the SQ8 dots, and block16: its int8 dot is built on 256-bit species, which the JVM cannot map to NEON (138 times slower than the scalar twin in CI, #52), and the other three need 8 float lanes. There Kernels uses the 128-bit forms of NKernels on aarch64 (Kernels.JVM_NARROW) and the scalar twins on any other host (Kernels.JVM_QUANT_SCALAR), and Kernels.quantReason says which and why. If NKernels cannot initialize on an aarch64 JVM, the scalar twins are used, never an exception. The fp32 dot and squared L2 stay in VKernels on every JVM, hamming stays scalar, and a JVM with 8 or more float lanes is unchanged. Kern.dotQ8 follows the same rule, so one run uses one SQ8 dot in the flat and in the graph tier. AVX-512 and SVE are not used.

Inside a GraalVM native image (Kernels.IN_IMAGE) the choice is different. VKernels is more than 10 times slower than scalar code there (a masked tail and a slice-based sum send the whole method through a slow path), so an image uses NKernels for every kernel that has a Vector API form (the fp32 dot and squared L2, the int8 dot, the SQ8 dots, and block16) when the module is present in the image, and the scalar twins otherwise. NKernels is the textbook form that an image compiles to SIMD code: a static final species, two accumulators, fma, reduceLanes(ADD), a scalar tail, no masks. The species is chosen from os.arch in a static initializer, 128 bits on aarch64 and 256 bits everywhere else (a CPU with AVX-512 runs the 256-bit species), and the image builder must run that initializer, which META-INF/native-image/ai.humem/tiervec/native-image.properties asks for with --initialize-at-build-time=ai.humem.tiervec.NKernels. The initializer catches a missing module and leaves the species null, so an image built without the module still builds and Kernels selects the scalar twins, with the cause in Kernels.scalarReason. The int8, SQ8, and block16 kernels have two forms each in NKernels, one per species, chosen by NKernels.WIDE: the wide form for the 256-bit float species, and the narrow form for the 128-bit one, where the Vector API has no 32-bit byte species, so the byte vector is loaded at 64 or 128 bits and split into parts. Each form is the one that was fastest in an image on both Oracle GraalVM 25 and GraalVM CE 25.0.2, on x86-64 and arm64 Linux (#48). Hamming has no Vector API form and stays scalar. Kernels.JVM_VECTOR and Kernels.NATIVE_VECTOR say which holder is in use. The fixed-order sum of the JVM kernels is not used in an image: a sum in a fixed order is fast only on Oracle GraalVM, so NKernels takes reduceLanes, and its result can differ from the JVM by rounding. To build the image, give the builder --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector -H:+VectorAPISupport (GraalVM 25; the properties file does not set them, so a scalar image stays possible).

Kern holds the graph kernels: float dot, squared L2, and the dot of a float query with SQ8 codes (in an image, NKernels.dotF8). Its Vector API versions are in VKern, and its scalar twins are the scalar twins of Kernels. Kern follows Kernels.VECTOR, and Kernels initializes both holder classes inside its try, so one run never mixes the two modes and a failure to load either holder selects the scalar twins for every index. GraphIndex, SealedGraph, and TieredIndex need no incubator class in that case.

A scalar result and a vector result of the same float kernel can differ by rounding. KernDiffTest states the tolerance (1e-5 times the sum of the absolute terms) and compares exactly representable data bit for bit; for NKernels it uses 1e-4 times the sum of the absolute terms plus a floor of 1e-6, on lengths around the lane width and at 100, 128, and 770, for every form of every NKernels kernel, so the 128-bit forms of aarch64 are tested on an x86 host too. NoIncubatorTest starts a JVM without the module and builds and searches a tier in it. The graph, segment, and tier tests also run with the scalar twins, in the surefire execution scalar-twin.

docs.title: Tier configuration
docs.text:
TieredIndex.Config is a record. Config.defaults() gives the defaults below, and with... methods return a changed copy. The constructor rejects tailLimit < 1, smallLimit < 0, maxSegments < 1, mergeFan < 2, hardTailFactor < 2, buildThreads < 1, a negative or infinite mergeTriggerRatio, and a BINARY tail quantizer.

Knob Default What it does tailLimit 2000 Seal when the active tail has this many vectors. tailAgeMs 60000 Also seal when the oldest tail vector is older than this. 0 means never by age. smallLimit 1000 Below this many live vectors no graph is ever built and every search is an exact scan. maxSegments 8 Merge when the segment count exceeds this. mergeFan 4 How many of the smallest segments one merge takes. deadFraction 0.3 Compact (merge) a segment when this share of it is hidden. mergeRatePerSec 50000 Insert rate cap of the merge builder. 0 means unlimited. hardTailFactor 4 Back pressure: writers wait when the active tail holds this factor times max(tailLimit, smallLimit) vectors. tailQuant NONE Tail kernel: NONE scans fp32, SQ8 scans int8 codes and reranks the best 5 times k candidates in fp32. graph GraphIndex.Params.defaults() Segment graph parameters: M 16, efConstruction 200, efSearch 100 (the search beam), alpha 1.0, sq8 false, seed 42. buildThreads max(1, min(4, cpus - 1)) Threads of one seal or merge build. splitBeam false When true and more than one segment is searched, segment s gets the beam max(k, ceil(ef * rows(s) / rows of all searched segments)) instead of the full ef. mergeTriggerRatio 0.0 Size-ratio merge trigger, off at 0. See below.

With mergeTriggerRatio X above 0, the segment with the most live rows is the big one. When the live rows of all the other segments together exceed X times the live rows of the big one, all segments are merged into one. Otherwise, if maxSegments is at least 2 and the count exceeds it, the count rule picks among the small segments only, so the big one is rewritten only by the ratio rule. With maxSegments 1 the count rule includes the big one and a merge happens at every seal. A merge into the big segment rewrites about (1 + X) / X vectors per inserted vector, on top of the small-segment merges.

Other controls on the tier: filterScanBelow(fraction) (default 0, off) is the scan-first threshold of filtered searches, applied per segment (the tails are always scanned exactly), sealNow(), mergeNow() and awaitIdle(timeoutMs) run or wait for the worker, search(q, k, allow, ef) sets the beam per call, and stats() reports seals, merges, segment sizes, floor entries, write amplification, and a log of finished tasks.

docs.title: Id epoch and replay
docs.text:
Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

This page specifies how a host numbers the vectors it gives to tiervec, how it tells the library that the numbering changed, and what the host and the library do after a restart. It belongs to the host contract and answers the questions that page leaves open about ids and recovery.

Status: specification, partly built. A piece is built only when it is marked exists today and names the test that shows it; everything else is planned. The tracking issues are #7 (epoch, snapshot rebuild, replay) and #9 (the manifest that stores the epoch). Nothing here is a measurement.

docs.title: Why it exists
docs.text:
The library keys every vector by an opaque long id that the host supplies. A host can renumber its ids (for example when it compacts its own storage), can reuse them, and can replay writes after a crash. A persisted segment that does not know which numbering its ids belong to can, after a restart, return the wrong vector for an id, and nobody notices. Without a replay protocol, every host invents its own recovery and gets the edge cases differently wrong.

The library is meant to hold derived data only. The vectors in the host's records are the truth, so every rule below is built to keep that true: whatever the library persisted can be checked against the records, and thrown away when the check fails.

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
• Id: the long that the host passes to add and delete and receives back in Hit.
  • Epoch: a long that names one numbering of ids. The library compares epochs only for equality and never orders them.
  • High-water id: the largest id held by any sealed segment of the persisted state. Every id in the tail is above it. This holds because a seal takes the whole frozen tail, and because add ids increase inside an epoch.
  • Recovered maximum: the highest id the host itself found after its own recovery.
  • Cold: an index with no usable persisted state. It is built from the host's records.

docs.title: Id models
docs.text:
Three models are possible. They differ in what the key is, and so in what the host and the library must do about reuse, ordering, and renumbering.

Stable host id plus epoch (recommended) Host record handle as the key Dense id that a compaction can reissue, with no epoch What the key is A long that the host mints per vector version, never reused inside an epoch, increasing for adds. The host's own record handle, packed into a long. The host's dense ordinal, 0 to n - 1, reissued in rank order when the host compacts. Width Fits a long by construction. A handle can be wider than 64 bits. Packing needs a width limit and an overflow check, and a wider key changes every id array in the segment format. Fits a long. Reuse of a record handle Impossible inside an epoch: a record that reuses its handle gets a new id. Possible. A freed handle can come back for another vector, so a delete and a later add carry the same key. Correct only through the version floor. Not an issue between compactions. Update An add of the new id plus a delete of the old id, in one batch. The floor degenerates to a set of dead ids. An add of the same key replaces the old copy, and the old copy is hidden by a floor raise. As the stable id, between compactions. Delete on disk delete(id). Tombstones on disk are an optimization, because open checks liveness. A floor raise per key. After a reopen the floor must be rebuilt from durable delete events in order, which needs a position in the host's log and an ordered iterator over it. As the stable id. Ordering rule for the library None: ids are unique. The host must send the delete before the add of the same key, and must supply a version per operation, because a counter inside the library reissues versions on replay. None, between compactions. Renumbering Detected: the epoch changes, and persisted state is discarded. A host that moves records changes keys, and nothing detects it. Not detected. Persisted state silently refers to the old numbering, and id 7 may now be another vector. What the library changes An epoch parameter on open and rebuild, and an epoch and a high-water id in the manifest. The in-memory tier is unchanged. A persisted floor, the key packing, and an optional section that carries the host's handle for each row, which can go stale. Nothing, and that is the problem. Residual risk The epoch must survive a crash that falls between the host's renumbering and the library's notice. Reuse across a reopen is closed only by replaying the host's log in order, which is host work. Persisted state is unsafe. Only a memory-only index, rebuilt at every open, is safe. A content fingerprint (live count, next id at the last checkpoint, a hash of the live ids in order) detects a renumbering with high probability and does not prove it.

The recommended model is the first. Reasons, all from the table: no reuse hazard inside an epoch, no width problem, no reconstruction of a floor from events the host may not store, a host mapping that usually exists already (the host finds a record from an id with a table it keeps), and no change to the in-memory tier.

exists today: the in-memory tier works with all three models, because the version floor hides old copies of a reused id (TieredIndex.add, TieredIndex.delete, DESIGN.md). Tests for reuse across seal and merge are planned (#5). The epoch and the high-water id are stored in the manifest and used at open (see the sections below).

With persistence on, one more rule follows from the high-water id. A host does not add a held id again with a different vector. In memory, the tier would replace it. After a reopen, the replay rule would miss a replaced vector whose id is at or below the high-water id, and the old copy could come back. A new vector version gets a new id. Adding a held id with the same vector is the replay case, and it is allowed.

docs.title: The epoch rule
docs.text:
1. The host passes an epoch to open and to rebuildFrom.
  2. The epoch changes whenever the host reissues or renumbers ids, including a compaction that renumbers, a restore from a backup that renumbers, and an import. It does not change when the host rebuilds an index and keeps its ids.
  3. Inside an epoch, the ids of adds strictly increase in the order the host applies them. Gaps are allowed. An id is not reused inside an epoch, not even after a delete.
  4. The manifest stores the epoch. At open, an epoch that differs from the host's gives a cold index. Persisted state is discarded as a whole, never partly reused.
  5. When the host renumbers while the library is running, it calls onRenumber(newEpoch) at the point where it reissues ids. The library drops its derived state and rebuilds in the new id space.
  6. The host persists the epoch together with its own data, in the same atomic step as the renumbering, so that a crash cannot leave new ids with the old epoch.

Rules 1 to 4 exists today: TieredIndex.rebuildFrom(Supplier<Snapshot>, long) and TieredIndex.open(dir, dim, metric, config, RecordSource) take the epoch, TieredIndex.checkpoint stores it in the manifest, and an open with another epoch gives a cold index. Tests: EpochReplayTest.rebuildFromTakesTheEpochAndTheSnapshotPosition, EpochReplayTest.theManifestStoresTheEpochAndTheHighWaterId, EpochReplayTest.anEpochMismatchGivesAColdIndex. A manifest of the previous layout (epoch unset, written by a tier that never had an epoch) still opens through open(dir, config), and a host that has an epoch gets a cold index from it (EpochReplayTest.aManifestOfThePreviousLayoutOpensAndGivesAColdIndexWhenTheHostHasAnEpoch, which also opens a manifest with a larger minor version). The manifest layout did not change, because it already had the two fields, so the format version did not change either. Long.MIN_VALUE is not a valid epoch: it is how the manifest says none. Rule 5: rebuildFrom(source, newEpoch) is the call that moves the library into a new numbering, with the tests above, and the host stops applying writes of the old numbering when it renumbers; a method named onRenumber is planned. Rule 6 is the host's side. The library relies on the order of ids and does not check it (planned, #7).

docs.title: The replay protocol
docs.text:
The host replays what the persisted state lacks, and the library reconciles what the host deleted or never made durable. This is the sequence after a restart, with the host's side marked as host.

  1. Host: finish the host's own recovery first, so that its records, its id table, and its recovered maximum are final. The library opens after that.
  2. Host: call open with the index definition, the configuration and its fingerprint, the environment, the record source, and the directory. The record source offers the epoch, every live record, every live record above a given id, a liveness test for one id, and the recovered maximum.
  3. Library: find the newest valid manifest. A damaged or truncated manifest falls back to the previous generation, and when none is usable the library throws CorruptStateException, so that the host calls rebuildFrom.
  4. Library: compare the manifest's fingerprint, dimension, metric, and epoch with the host's. Any mismatch gives a cold index and ends the sequence here.
  5. Library: apply the durable-prefix rule. Every held id above the recovered maximum is dropped (see below).
  6. Library: for every id still held in a segment, ask the record source whether the id is live. A record that is not live marks the row dead. This is a check per held id, not a scan of the host's pages.
  7. Library: ask the record source for every live record above the high-water id, in increasing id order, and append the vectors to the tail. Segments are not touched.
  8. Library: report ready. The host resumes normal traffic: one apply per committed transaction.

If the persisted state is cold, the host calls rebuildFrom over its live records, with its epoch and a snapshot position, and the library reports ready when the build is swapped in.

Rebuild while the host keeps writing: the host passes a snapshot position, which is the highest id covered by the records it hands over. The library builds without blocking apply or search. Adds above the snapshot position that arrive during the build are kept and applied after the swap. Deletes that arrive during the build are kept as well, in arrival order, and applied after the swap, so that a delete of an id that the snapshot contains is not lost. None is lost and none is applied twice. exists today: TieredIndex.rebuildFrom(Supplier<Snapshot>, long), and the form rebuildFrom(records, epoch, snapshotPosition). The text above does not say who starts first, the host's snapshot or the library's record of writes. The order that is safe is: the library starts to record the writes it accepts, then asks the host for the snapshot. A write that the host applied before the library started to record, and that the snapshot does not cover, would be lost. So the host takes its snapshot inside the supplier that the library calls, and serializes that with its own calls of apply. At the swap, under one hold of the write lock, the recorded writes are applied to the rebuilt state in arrival order, adds at or below the snapshot position skipped, and recording stops. Tests: EpochReplayTest.writesThatArriveDuringTheBuildAreKeptAndAppliedAfterTheSwap (a write from another thread gets through during the build, adds above the position are kept once, deletes of ids of the snapshot are applied, and a late batch at or below the position is not applied again), EpochReplayTest.anAbortedRebuildChangesNothing, EpochReplayStressTest.aRebuildNeverLosesAWriteThatArrivesDuringIt (a host thread writes without a pause while the tier is rebuilt from snapshots), and its long variant in EpochReplayLongTest. The one-argument rebuildFrom(Iterable<IdVector>) is unchanged: it holds the write lock for the whole build and keeps the epoch.

Steps 3 to 8 exists today as TieredIndex.open(dir, dim, metric, config, RecordSource), with these differences from the text above. The fingerprint, the dimension, the metric, and the epoch are compared, and any failure to read the directory (damage, a newer format, no manifest) gives a cold index with the cause in openFallbackCause(), where step 3 says the library throws CorruptStateException; that class does not exist yet ([#18]). The replay of step 7 is applied with apply in batches of 1024. Step 8 is the return of open. Tests: EpochReplayTest.theHostReplaysEverythingAboveTheHighWaterId, EpochReplayTest.theLivenessCheckHidesIdsTheHostDeleted (the rows are hidden in memory only, and a liveness check alone writes nothing), EpochReplayTest.idsAboveTheRecoveredMaximumAreDroppedBeforeTheIndexIsReady.

docs.title: The idempotence rule
docs.text:
add of a held id replaces it with the same vector, and delete of an absent id returns false and changes nothing. Re-applying a batch therefore changes nothing visible, on one condition that the host guarantees: inside an epoch, an id always denotes one vector.

Because of this, the host may start a replay at or below the true position. A replay that starts too early is slower, never wrong. This is what lets the high-water id lag, and what makes a crash in the middle of a replay harmless.

exists today for single calls: TieredIndex.add, TieredIndex.delete. exists today for whole batches: TieredIndex.apply, tested by ApplyBatchTest.applyingTheSameBatchAgainChangesNothingVisible. exists today across a checkpoint and a reopen: EpochReplayTest.replayingTheSameBatchesAfterAReopenChangesNothing applies the batches of the host again, in order, after open.

docs.title: The durable-prefix rule
docs.text:
A commit can count as final in the host's view and still miss the disk (for example under an asynchronous log flush). A segment that the library persisted earlier can then hold an id that the host forgot and hands to another record after the restart.

Ids increase in the order in which the host applies batches, so the ids the host lost are exactly the ids above its recovered maximum. At open, the library drops every held id above that maximum.

Two consequences follow from the way the library persists state. They are part of the rule.

  • Dead is sticky. A row that an open or an apply has marked dead stays dead in every later generation. A liveness check may kill rows and never revives one. Otherwise, after the host mints a new record with a dropped id, a later open would find that id live again and bring back the old vector.
  • The high-water id is lowered to the recovered maximum when rows are dropped. The host may mint the dropped ids again for new records, and those records must lie above the high-water id, so that a later replay finds them.
  • The drop must be durable before the library reports ready, or the library discards the persisted state and goes cold. The library may always choose cold. The first implementation may do so whenever the rule drops a row.

exists today, without the shortcut: TieredIndex.open(dir, dim, metric, config, RecordSource) drops every held id above recoveredMax(), rebuilds the segments without those rows (mergeNow), and publishes a new generation (checkpoint) before it returns; when that fails the tier goes cold. The high-water id of the new generation is the largest id that the remaining segments hold, which is at most the recovered maximum. Dead is sticky because a dropped row is in no later generation. A row that the liveness check hides stays in the older files only, and every open asks again, which is safe because an id is not reused inside an epoch. The recovered maximum is the highest id that the host found when it recovered, not the highest id it holds when it calls open: a host that minted new records in between passes the older value, and the tier then drops the persisted copies of those ids and replays the new records (a host that passes its current maximum keeps the old vectors under the re-minted ids, which is a host error that the library cannot see). Tests: EpochReplayTest.idsAboveTheRecoveredMaximumAreDroppedBeforeTheIndexIsReady (the host forgets 40 adds and mints the same ids again for other vectors: this open and a later one return the new vectors only, and a reader that knows nothing about the host finds none of the lost rows), EpochReplayStressTest.crashAndReopenLoop, and its long variant in EpochReplayLongTest.

The rule covers adds. It does not say what happens to a delete that the library persisted (a compacted segment) and the host then forgot: the record is live again in the host, with an id at or below the recovered maximum, and no segment holds it any more, so nothing replays it. The tests keep to the safer reading: the host makes its deletes durable before it lets the library checkpoint (FakeHost.flushDeletes). The contract needs a sentence on this from the host's side, or a decision that the library refuses to persist a delete that the host has not confirmed.

docs.title: What a crash leaves, at each point
docs.text:
A process kill is assumed. No claim is made about power loss until a test says otherwise (#17).

The crash falls What is durable What the next open does In the host, before its commit is durable Nothing of this batch, in the host or in the library. Nothing to do. The library never saw the batch, because the host applies only when changes stand. After the host's commit is durable and before apply ran The host's records. Step 7 of the replay: the live records above the high-water id come back into the tail. After apply, before any seal The host's records. The tail was in memory only. As above. During a seal or merge, before the new manifest is durable The previous generation, plus an orphan segment file. The previous generation opens. The orphan is deleted. The records above its high-water id are replayed. After a new manifest is durable, and the host lost the commit that its segment holds A segment that holds ids the host no longer has. The durable-prefix rule drops the ids above the recovered maximum. After a delete was applied in memory and before a manifest recorded it The host's records without the record. Step 6: the liveness check marks the row dead. During a rebuild The previous persisted state. A rebuild replaces state only at the swap and publishes a new manifest after it. The previous state opens, or the host rebuilds again. After the host renumbered, before the library heard of it The host's new numbering and its epoch, if it persisted them with the renumbering (rule 6). Old segments with the old epoch. The epoch differs, so the index is cold and the host rebuilds. In the middle of a replay Nothing new. A replay changes nothing durable until the next publish. The same replay again. It is idempotent. A segment or manifest is damaged Whatever damage the file has. CorruptStateException, and the host calls rebuildFrom. A second failure is a host error.

exists today for a process kill: EpochReplayTest.aCrashAtEveryStepOfAPublishLeavesAnIndexThatMatchesTheHost runs the fault hook after each of the six publish steps, and EpochReplayStressTest.crashAndReopenLoop crashes the host and the tier at random points (sometimes in the middle of a publish) and checks after every reopen that the tier holds exactly the host's live records, each with the host's vector. The row for a crash in the middle of a replay has no test of its own: a replay changes nothing durable, and applying a batch again is tested. No claim is made about power loss (#17).

docs.title: Open questions for a host
docs.text:
A host answers these before it relies on the protocol. A different answer changes a rule above.

  1. Can the host persist an epoch atomically with any renumbering of its ids? If it cannot, the library has only the content fingerprint, which detects a renumbering with high probability and does not prove it, and the host must accept a rebuild after every compaction, or a memory-only index.
  2. Does the host report every path that reissues ids? Compaction is the obvious one. A restore from a backup, an import, a rebuild of the host's own tables, and the installation of a replica's snapshot are others.
  3. Are ids minted in the order in which the host applies batches, even with concurrent transactions? The rule needs a strictly increasing order, so the host serializes apply per index and mints in that order, or it mints under a lock that gives the same order.
  4. Can the host list its live records above a given id without scanning everything, and test one id for liveness in constant time? The cost of step 6 and step 7 is the cost of these two calls.
  5. Can the host tell the highest id it recovered after a crash? Under which flush modes can a commit that it counted as final be lost?
  6. Does the host call apply only when changes stand? If it must apply earlier, it must undo an add with a delete and a delete with an add of the vector, and the persisted state then may contain ids of transactions that did not stand, which only the durable-prefix rule covers.
  7. When does the host open the index relative to its own recovery? The library needs final records.
  8. What does a replica, a restored copy, or a copy from a backup contain? The library's files may be absent or older than the records. Absent files give a cold index.
  9. How much memory does the staging of a long transaction hold until it applies? The library does not bound that.

docs.title: Host contract
docs.text:
Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

This page states what a database (the host) must provide to embed tiervec, and what tiervec guarantees in return. It is written for an engine developer who reviews the contract before writing an adapter. The word provider appears in the file name: tiervec is the provider of a vector index, and the host is the database that calls it.

The library is experimental and is not wired into any database yet. Most lines below describe where the library is going, not where it is. Every line carries a mark, so a reader can tell a promise from a plan. Nothing here is a measurement: measurements will be published with the harness.

Two companion pages go deeper where a topic is large: ID-EPOCH-AND-REPLAY.md for ids, epochs, and recovery after a crash, and DESIGN.md for what the code does today.

docs.title: Purpose and non-goals
docs.text:
A host that embeds an index has to know what is atomic, who sees a write and when, which calls may block, which threads the library creates, and what happens after a crash. This page is the one place where those answers live, so a reviewer does not have to read the code.

The contract is written in host terms and names no particular database. The host-side interfaces use only long, float[], Map<String, String>, java.util.concurrent.Executor, and java.util.function types, so the library needs no dependency on any database.

Non-goals:

  • Transactions. The library has no rollback and no notion of uncommitted rows. They stay on the host side.
  • Record storage. The host's records are the source of truth. Everything the library keeps is derived and can be rebuilt from them.
  • A query language, a server, or a network. The host parses its own queries and hands the library vectors and allowed-id sets.
  • Ordering across several indexes.

docs.title: Reading the marks
docs.text:
• exists today: built on the main branch at the time of writing, and checked by a test that the status table at the end names. The class and method are named.
  • partly: a form of the guarantee exists, or it is built and no dedicated test checks it. The line says what is missing.
  • planned: not built. The issue number is the tracking issue, and the acceptance test in that issue is the bar.

Names of planned interfaces and methods are descriptive, not final. The Java package is ai.humem.tiervec.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
What the host must provide:

  1. Ids: an opaque long per vector version, minted by the host, unique inside an epoch, and strictly increasing for adds inside an epoch. The epoch changes whenever the host renumbers.
  2. Apply order: one batch per committed transaction per index, applied only when the transaction's changes stand, serialized per index.
  3. Records: a way to read every live record, to ask whether an id is live, and to learn the highest id the host itself recovered after a crash.
  4. Resources: an executor, a build permit, and a memory budget, so the library creates no thread of its own, and a capacity check before each batch.
  5. Transactions: the overlay of uncommitted rows, the mapping from ids to the host's records, and the translation of the host's filters into an allowed-id predicate.

What tiervec guarantees:

  1. A batch is visible as a unit. After apply returns, a search that starts later sees the adds and not the deletes, and applying the same batch again changes nothing visible.
  2. A search returns at most k hits, best first, with no duplicate id and no id deleted before the search started. The allowed-id predicate is applied inside the search. The query path takes no lock and creates no thread, but a search waits while a batch is being applied (see apply(batch)).
  3. A search stops at a deadline or a cancel flag that the host supplies.
  4. After a reopen, the persisted state is either reconciled with the host's records or discarded in favor of a rebuild. It never returns a vector for an id that now means a different vector.
  5. Errors are unchecked and classified, and a contract version and a capability set tell the host what exists.

docs.title: Roles and host interfaces
docs.text:
The library defines three small interfaces for itself. A separate adapter, outside the library core, implements them on top of the host's own classes. No host class appears in the library's API.

Interface What the host supplies Status Environment An executor for every seal, merge, and build task. A build permit: ask with a kind and an estimate of peak bytes, receive a permit or a refusal. A memory budget in bytes, read at each decision. A metric sink with counters and gauges. planned (#13) Record source The host's epoch. Every live record. Every live record with an id above a given id. A liveness test for one id. The highest id the host recovered after its own crash. exists today: RecordSource, used by TieredIndex.open, tested by EpochReplayTest with a fake host Search context A deadline and a cancel flag, polled by the library during a search. planned (#11)

Today the library has none of the three. It runs one worker thread and, during a seal or a merge, a few build threads (Config.buildThreads), and it reads its records only through add and rebuildFrom.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
Each row names who does what. "Host" is the adapter on the host side, "library" is tiervec.

Operation Host does Library guarantees Status add(id, vector) and delete(id), single calls Calls them with the rules of the identity section. Each call is atomic and visible to the next search in any thread. add of a held id replaces its vector. delete returns true when the id existed. exists today: TieredIndex.add, TieredIndex.delete, VecIndex apply(batch) Calls it with an ordered list of adds and deletes, once per committed transaction per index, serialized per index, with add ids strictly increasing inside the epoch. The whole batch becomes visible together: adds are applied before deletes, under one hold of the write lock, and a search sees all of the batch or none of it. Re-applying a batch changes nothing visible. A search that overlaps a batch waits for it or runs again, so a batch can delay a search by its own length. exists today: TieredIndex.apply. Tests: ApplyBatchTest (visibility, a search held across a batch, re-apply), ApplyStressTest (slow: updater and searcher threads) awaitCapacity(deadline) Calls it before apply, outside any lock of its own. Waits for room in the tail or returns false. apply itself never sleeps on the library's maintenance. The behavior at the hard tail limit is defined and tested: apply does not look at the limit, and one batch may take the tail above it. exists today: TieredIndex.awaitCapacity, with the deadline on the System.nanoTime() clock. Test: ApplyBatchTest.behaviorAtTheHardTailLimit. The single call TieredIndex.add keeps its own wait of up to 10 s at the hard limit search(query, k, allowed, context) Passes the query, k, an allowed-id predicate (optionally with a size hint), and a search context. At most k hits, best first, no duplicate id, no deleted id, fewer than k only when fewer qualify. A search stops when the context says so. exists today without the context: TieredIndex.search, three overloads. Context: planned (#11). Size hint: planned (#12) open(config, fingerprint, environment, record source, directory) Passes the index definition (dimension, metric), the configuration, its fingerprint, the interfaces above, and a directory that only this node uses (or none, for memory only). Returns ready or cold. A mismatch of fingerprint, dimension, metric, or epoch discards persisted state and returns cold, never a wrong answer. partly: TieredIndex.open(dir, dim, metric, config, RecordSource) checks the epoch, drops ids above the recovered maximum, hides ids that are not live, and replays the live records above the high-water id (EpochReplayTest). It takes no environment and no fingerprint string (#18), it needs a directory, and a cold index is built on the calling thread (#13) awaitReady(deadline) Calls it before the first search of a cold index, and from its own warm-up hook. Builds from the record source on the host executor under a host permit, never on the caller's query thread unless the caller asks for that. planned (#9, #13) rebuildFrom(records, epoch, snapshot position) Calls it for a first build, a rebuild, the fallback after corruption, and after a renumbering. Replaces all derived state without blocking apply or search. Adds and deletes that arrive during the build are kept and applied after the swap. Streams the records instead of copying them first. exists today for the epoch, the snapshot position, and the catch-up: TieredIndex.rebuildFrom(Supplier<Snapshot>, long) and rebuildFrom(records, epoch, snapshotPosition), tested by EpochReplayTest.writesThatArriveDuringTheBuildAreKeptAndAppliedAfterTheSwap and EpochReplayStressTest.aRebuildNeverLosesAWriteThatArrivesDuringIt. partly for the rest: the build copies all records into a map first instead of streaming them and runs on the calling thread (#13), and the swap holds the write lock while the recorded writes are applied. The form rebuildFrom(Iterable) still holds the write lock for the whole build flush() Calls it where the host flushes its own indexes. Writes the manifest and any dirty state, returns when durable, idempotent. planned (#9) close() Calls it when the host closes the index. Stops accepting work, waits for or cancels the tasks it submitted, releases files, idempotent, never creates a thread. partly: TieredIndex.close() stops the worker thread and a second call is harmless. No defined behavior for searches in flight. Rest: planned (#13, #18) drop() and clear() Calls drop when the index is deleted and clear when its data is truncated. Removes every file it wrote and all in-memory state, idempotent. planned (#9) verify() Calls it from the host's own integrity check. Returns a list of problems and never throws for a damaged file. planned (#9, #17) onRenumber(newEpoch) Calls it at the point where it reissues ids. Drops derived state and rebuilds in the new id space. partly: rebuildFrom(source, newEpoch) does it. onRenumber as a named call is not built, and the host stops applying writes of the old numbering when it renumbers metrics Reads it into its own statistics. A map of counters and gauges, plus an optional push sink. partly: TieredIndex.stats() returns a Stats record. Map and sink: planned (#18) contractVersion(), capabilities(), health() Checks them at creation and when index metadata changes. A major and a minor number, a capability set, and a health state. planned (#18) Suspend and resume of background maintenance Calls it around a bulk load. No seal or merge starts while suspended. apply still works. planned, no issue filed yet

docs.title: Identity and the epoch
docs.text:
The library keys every vector by an opaque long id that the host supplies. The id is not a record id of the host: a record id can be reused after a delete, can be wider than 64 bits, and can change when the host moves a record. An id inside an epoch cannot be reused.

  • The host mints ids. They are unique inside an epoch, and the ids of adds strictly increase inside an epoch. Gaps are allowed. exists today: ids are plain long values in VecIndex.add, Hit, and TieredIndex.IdVector. A check of the ordering rule is planned (#7): the library relies on it for the high-water id and does not verify it.
  • An update is a new id plus a delete of the old id, sent in one batch. The library needs nothing special for it: two ids, and the delete hides the old copy. exists today as one batch (TieredIndex.apply) and as two calls.
  • The epoch names one numbering of ids. The host passes it to open and rebuildFrom. The manifest stores it. A different epoch means persisted state is discarded and the index starts cold. exists today: EpochReplayTest.anEpochMismatchGivesAColdIndex and EpochReplayTest.theManifestStoresTheEpochAndTheHighWaterId.
  • A host that reuses ids anyway (a record id used directly as the key) is served in memory by the version floor: an id added after a delete is visible, and the old copies stay hidden. partly: TieredIndex.add, TieredIndex.delete, and the floor described in DESIGN.md are built, and the tests cover replace, not delete followed by add of the same id. Tests for reuse across seal and merge are planned (#5). Persisting such a tier is not covered by this contract.

The id models, their consequences, and the open questions are in ID-EPOCH-AND-REPLAY.md.

docs.title: Mutation, replay, and ordering
docs.text:
• Idempotence. add of a held id replaces it with the same vector, and delete of an absent id returns false and changes nothing. A host may therefore replay a batch after a crash, and replaying one that was already applied changes nothing visible. exists today for single calls: TieredIndex.add, TieredIndex.delete. exists today for whole batches: TieredIndex.apply, tested by ApplyBatchTest.applyingTheSameBatchAgainChangesNothingVisible.
  • Order. Inside a batch, adds are applied before deletes. Across batches, the host serializes calls per index. The library needs no remove-before-add rule, because ids are unique. exists today: TieredIndex.apply, tested by ApplyBatchTest.theWholeBatchIsVisibleAfterApplyReturns (an id that one batch adds and deletes ends deleted).
  • Apply at commit, or apply after validation. The recommended host behavior is to stage a transaction's changes and call apply only when the changes stand. The library then never sees an id of a rolled-back transaction and needs no retract operation. The reason is that a sealed segment is immutable and can be made durable on its own schedule: a row applied too early and then rolled back can be sealed before the rollback runs. The floor hides it from results, but the segment still holds a row for an id the host has forgotten, and the host may hand that id to another record after a restart. The library has no transaction notion, so nothing in it contradicts deferred apply. exists today on the library side, as a property of the code with nothing to test. Staging is the adapter's job.
  • A host that cannot defer can undo an add with delete and undo a delete by adding the vector again. The version floor makes that correct in memory. The library has no retract operation. The capability set will say which style a given library version supports. planned (#18).
  • Replay after a reopen: the host replays every live record above the manifest's high-water id, and the library checks liveness of every id it holds. Specified in ID-EPOCH-AND-REPLAY.md. exists today: TieredIndex.open(dir, dim, metric, config, RecordSource), tested by EpochReplayTest.theHostReplaysEverythingAboveTheHighWaterId and EpochReplayTest.theLivenessCheckHidesIdsTheHostDeleted.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
• Arguments: a query vector, k, an allowed-id predicate (or none), and a context. An optional effort knob sets the beam width of the segment search. A non-positive k returns an empty result. exists today without the context: TieredIndex.search(float[], int, LongPredicate), search(..., Freshness), search(..., int ef).
  • Result: at most k hits, best first, each Hit(id, score), no duplicate ids. Fewer than k only when fewer live vectors qualify. exists today: VecIndex.search, Hit.
  • Score: higher is better for every metric. Cosine and dot are returned as they are, L2 as the negative squared distance. A host whose engine uses a distance where lower is better converts, and checks the conversion with a parity test on the same data. exists today: Hit. A public scorer for a single pair of vectors, which a host needs to score its own uncommitted rows with the same arithmetic, is planned, no issue filed yet.
  • Exactness flag: SearchResult.exact tells the host that no segment was searched and the tail scan was exact. exists today: TieredIndex.search(..., Freshness).
  • Allowed-id predicate. The host supplies a LongPredicate. It must be cheap, side-effect free, safe to call more than once for the same id, and it must not call back into the index. The library applies it inside the segment search and the tail scan, so the top k of the qualifying set is correct, and a graph walk with few qualifying ids falls back to an exact scan after a visit budget. exists today: the predicate parameter of TieredIndex.search. Correctness of filtered search is checked by unit tests. How it behaves across the range of selectivities has not been measured. An optional size hint and a live count, so that a small allowed set is scanned exactly, are planned (#12).
  • Context. The library polls the context at a fixed, documented interval inside the tail scan and the segment search and between segments, and throws SearchCancelledException when it says stop. planned (#11, #18).
  • Threads and locks. A search runs on the calling thread, takes no lock, and never waits for a seal, a merge, or the build of a rebuild. It can be delayed by a batch in progress, for the length of that batch (it waits until the batch is whole, and scans again when a batch overlapped its scan; see apply(batch)), and by the swap of a snapshot rebuild together with its catch-up. A stream of batches that follow each other faster than one scan takes can starve it. partly: built in TieredIndex.search and stated in its class documentation, and ApplyBatchTest checks the wait for a batch, but no dedicated test checks the rest.
  • Freshness. By default a search sees the tails, so a write is visible at once. Freshness.SEALED_ONLY skips the tails and may lag. It never returns a deleted id, a stale vector, or an id that was never added. exists today: TieredIndex.Freshness.

docs.title: Visibility and publish
docs.text:
• The writing transaction sees its own uncommitted rows through the host's overlay. Any other session sees nothing before commit. After commit, the batch is visible from the moment apply returns. A host that calls apply before it tells its client the commit is done gives that client read-your-writes. The overlay is the adapter's job, see the last section.
  • The segment list, the active tail, and the frozen tail live in one immutable view. A seal or a merge publishes a new view with one volatile write, and a search reads the view once. exists today: the view inside TieredIndex.
  • An in-flight search finishes on the view it read, and retired segments stay valid until the last reader leaves. In memory, garbage collection does that. partly: there is no dedicated test of a long search across a swap. A memory-mapped reader would need a reference count before it unmaps, and none is planned yet.
  • Seal and merge never block a search, and block add, delete, and apply only for a short critical section. exists today for seal, merge, and rebuildFrom(Supplier<Snapshot>, long), whose swap holds the write lock for the catch-up (EpochReplayTest.writesThatArriveDuringTheBuildAreKeptAndAppliedAfterTheSwap lets a write from another thread through during the build). partly for the one-argument rebuildFrom(Iterable), which holds the write lock for the whole build.
  • Close with searches in flight: later calls throw ClosedException, and an in-flight search finishes or throws it, never returning a wrong id. planned (#18).

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
• Open: the host opens after its own recovery has finished, so the records and ids it exposes are final. The result is ready or cold.
  • Readiness: a cold index is built from the record source, on the host executor, under a host permit.
  • Rebuild from records: always available, and always correct, because the vectors in the host's records are the truth. It is the answer to every integrity failure.
  • Flush, close, drop, clear, and verify: as in the operations table.
  • Files: a host may keep the library's files outside its own storage. The library never registers a file with the host's storage manager, writes only inside the directory it is given, and treats a restored or replicated copy that has no files as a cold index. planned (#9).
  • Persistence: the format, as the first cut writes it, is in SEGMENT-FORMAT.md. A settled tier is written by TieredIndex.checkpoint and read by TieredIndex.open. The tests for damaged files and crashes at scale are #17.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
• After a restart the host replays what the persisted state lacks, and the library reconciles what the host deleted or never made durable. The steps, the high-water id, the liveness check, and the durable-prefix rule are in ID-EPOCH-AND-REPLAY.md. exists today for a process kill: EpochReplayTest.aCrashAtEveryStepOfAPublishLeavesAnIndexThatMatchesTheHost and EpochReplayStressTest.crashAndReopenLoop.
  • Requirement on the host, write-ahead: the index is never ahead of the host's durable log. A checkpoint may cover only transactions that the host has already made durable. If the library persisted a delete (a compacted segment) that the host then forgot in a crash, the record is live again in the host with an id at or below the recovered maximum and no segment holds it, and no rule of the library repairs that.
