The library cannot check the requirement, so a host that calls checkpoint before its own flush has a host error; the host that flushes first never sees the case. A library-side refusal to persist an unconfirmed delete is not built. exists today as a requirement; the test host of EpochReplayStressTest follows it.
  • Any integrity failure at open throws, and the host calls rebuildFrom. A second failure is a host error. partly: TieredIndex.open throws SegmentFormat.CorruptException, a checked IOException (and UnsupportedException, MismatchException, NoSuchFileException), and an overload that takes a rebuild source does the fallback. The unchecked CorruptStateException of the error classes is #18.
  • The claim: a process kill leaves the last published generation or the one before it. No claim is made about power loss until a test says otherwise. planned (#17).

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
• No thread of the library's own. Every seal, merge, and build task, including the parallel part of a build, goes to the host executor. partly: today TieredIndex starts one worker thread and, per build, a few threads (Config.buildThreads). planned (#13).
  • Build permit. Before each seal, merge, and rebuild the library asks for a permit with an estimate of peak bytes, computed from the sizes of the segments involved. On refusal it defers and retries with back-off, and never builds without a permit. planned (#13).
  • Memory budget. The library keeps its resident bytes below the budget by deferring merges and shrinking its tail limit. partly: TieredIndex.bytesHeld() reports resident bytes, and nothing reads a budget yet. planned (#13).
  • Throttle. The insert rate of a merge build is capped (Config.mergeRatePerSec). It is a politeness limit for the threads that serve queries, not a substitute for a permit. partly: built, and no dedicated test checks the cap.
  • Back pressure is a pre-check (awaitCapacity), and the tail is bounded. partly: TieredIndex.awaitCapacity is built and tested. The bound is soft: apply does not look at it, so one batch can take the tail above the hard limit, and TieredIndex.add adds after its own wait of up to 10 s.
  • No search-time thread creation, and no allocation proportional to the collection size on the query path. partly: built in TieredIndex.search, and no dedicated test checks it.
  • The graph kernels need the jdk.incubator.vector module at run time. The graph kernels have a scalar twin that is used when the module is absent, exists today: KernDiffTest compares the vector and the scalar kernel, and NoIncubatorTest builds and searches a tier in a JVM without the module. A native-image build of the library and a smoke program is checked by the workflow native-image.yml (the job native image smoke, and the vector variant native image smoke (vector, ...) on x86-64 and arm64 Linux), exists today, not a required check. In a native image the graph kernels (dot, squared L2, and the SQ8 dot) use the Vector API through NKernels with a build-time species, and a score can differ from the JVM by rounding.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• The library reads its configuration from a Map<String, String> and a fingerprint. The fingerprint is a canonical string and a hash over the data-affecting settings only: dimension, metric, id width, graph parameters, segment quantization, and layer layout. Search-time knobs (the beam width, the split-beam switch) and the settings of the tail are not part of it, because the tail is not persisted. planned (#18).
  • The host stores the fingerprint in its index metadata and passes it back at open. A mismatch discards persisted state.
  • Unknown keys are rejected at creation with the key named, and ignored with a warning at load, so a downgrade still opens.
  • Search-time knobs may change at run time. Data-affecting keys may not.
  • partly: the typed TieredIndex.Config record with validation, with... copies, and Config.defaults() is built, and no dedicated test checks the validation. The knobs are in DESIGN.md.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
• A pull form: a Map<String, Long> of counters and gauges. A push form: a sink with counter(name) and gauge(name, supplier). Names are prefixed tiervec.. No metrics library is a dependency. planned (#18).
  • The quantities are the ones TieredIndex.Stats holds today: seals, merges, failures, back-pressure waits, tail size, segment count, bytes held, floor entries, and write amplification (a gauge in thousandths). partly: TieredIndex.stats().

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• Unchecked only. The base is a provider exception. Classes: CorruptStateException (the host falls back to rebuildFrom), SearchCancelledException, ClosedException, and BuildRefusedException. Programming errors stay IllegalArgumentException and IllegalStateException. partly: the two standard exceptions exist today (a dimension mismatch throws IllegalArgumentException). The classified family is planned (#18).
  • A background failure never throws into apply or search. It is counted, kept as the last error, and retried. A health state reports ok, degraded (a task failing repeatedly), or failed (the worker is dead). partly: TieredIndex.lastError(), TieredIndex.workerAlive(), and the failures count in Stats. planned (#18).

docs.title: Versioning and capabilities
docs.text:
• The contract has a major and a minor number. The host refuses a library with a larger major. A larger minor is accepted, and capabilities it does not know are ignored. New operations are added as default methods. planned (#18).
  • The segment file and the manifest have their own version numbers, under the same rule. planned (#6, #9).
  • Capabilities are a bit set: deferred apply, selective plan, persistence, and snapshot rebuild, with more as they appear. The host checks them at creation. planned (#18).
  • What tiervec does not offer, so a host can refuse such an index definition at creation and not at query time: grouped (per-group top k) search, and approximate scores from compressed codes without an exact rescoring pass. Returned scores are exact fp32 scores. exists today as a fact about the code. The check through capabilities is planned (#18).

docs.title: What a host adapter typically does
docs.text:
The adapter is the host's code. It sits between the host's classes and the library, and it is where the host's own concepts end.

  • Key mapping. The adapter keeps a table from library id to the host's record handle, and mints a new id for every new vector version. A hit costs one lookup in that table. An update sends an add of the new id and a delete of the old id in one batch.
  • Overlay of uncommitted rows. The library has no transaction notion. For a search inside an open transaction, the adapter scores that transaction's pending rows exactly, with the same metric, merges them with the library's hits by score, and masks the ids the transaction has superseded by excluding them in the allowed-id predicate.
  • Allowed-id bridging. The host's filter produces a set of record handles. The adapter wraps it as a LongPredicate over library ids: map the id to its record handle, then test membership. It passes a size hint when it knows one.
  • Staging. The adapter holds a transaction's adds and deletes until the changes stand, then calls apply once.
  • Recovery glue. The adapter implements the record source on top of the host's own record scan and id table, and persists the epoch beside its own data.
  • Conversion. If the host reports distances where lower is better, the adapter converts scores, and a parity test on the same data checks the conversion.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

This page is the rule for version numbers and the steps of a release. The first release is 0.1.0. Between releases the version on main is the next -SNAPSHOT.

docs.title: Version numbers
docs.text:
• A release version is 0.MINOR.PATCH while the API is not stable. At 1.0 it becomes MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.
  • A breaking change to the supported surface needs a new MINOR version. A release that has none can be a new PATCH version. The rule and the meaning of "breaking" are in API.md.
  • Between releases main carries a -SNAPSHOT version, as Maven expects. After 0.1.0, main is 0.1.1-SNAPSHOT. When the first breaking change lands, main moves to 0.2.0-SNAPSHOT.
  • There is no .devN, aN, bN or rcN form. Maven does not order 0.1.0-dev1 before 0.1.0: it sorts an unknown qualifier after the release. A pre-release is a -SNAPSHOT.
  • A tag is the bare version, for example 0.1.0, with no v.
  • The version has one source: the <version> line in pom.xml.

docs.title: What a release has
docs.text:
• A tag on the commit of main that carries the release version.
  • A section in CHANGELOG.md with the version and the date.
  • A GitHub release whose notes are that section.
  • A documentation version <version> with the alias latest at https://docs.humem.ai/tiervec/. The tag push publishes it (workflow deploy-docs.yml). A push to main publishes only dev.
  • The artifact ai.humem:tiervec:<version> on Maven Central: the jar, a sources jar and a javadoc jar, each signed. Publishing the GitHub release starts everything (workflow release-central.yml): the upload, the publication by the Central Portal, and a check of the result on repo1.maven.org. Nobody presses a button in the portal. The details are in the section "Maven Central" below (#62).

docs.title: The changelog
docs.text:
CHANGELOG.md follows the "Keep a Changelog" layout: a section Unreleased at the top, then one section per release, newest first. The groups in a section are Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed and Security.

A pull request that changes the supported surface, the file format, or a documented guarantee adds its line to Unreleased in the same pull request. A breaking change says so and says what to change. A change in the file format says which older readers refuse the new files (SEGMENT-FORMAT.md).

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
Only the maintainer tags and publishes a release.

  1. Check that the latest commit on main is green: every check of its run is SUCCESS (a skipped check is fine). Do not release from a red or running main.
  2. Create the branch release/<version> from that commit.
  3. In pom.xml, change <version> to the release version (no -SNAPSHOT).
  4. In CHANGELOG.md, rename Unreleased to <version> - YYYY-MM-DD, add an empty Unreleased above it, and read the entry once against git log <previous tag>..HEAD.
  5. Update docs/STATUS.md and the README status table where the release changes what they say (for example the line "A release: none").
  6. Run the Central dry run on the branch and read its result (see "Maven Central" below):
gh workflow run release-central.yml --ref release/<version> -f dry-run=true
  1. Open a pull request named Release <version>, wait for green, and merge it.
  2. Tag the merge commit and push the tag. The tag is the bare version:
git tag <version> <merge-sha>
git push origin <version>

The tag push starts the workflow Deploy docs. It publishes the documentation as <version> with the alias latest, and latest is the default of the site.

  1. Publish the GitHub release. The notes are the changelog section of this version:
gh release create <version> --title <version> --notes-file <file with the section>

Publishing the release is the last manual act. It starts the workflow Release to Maven Central, which does the rest.

  1. Wait for the workflow Release to Maven Central to finish green:

    gh run list --workflow release-central.yml --limit 1
gh run watch <run-id> --exit-status

    It builds from the tag, signs, uploads the bundle, lets the Central Portal publish it, waits for the files on repo1.maven.org and verifies them (the section "The publish run" below has the list). There is nothing to press in the portal. A green run means that ai.humem:tiervec:<version> resolves from Maven Central, which is the done-when of issue #62: the first green run comments on that issue and closes it. A red run is read in its log; "The publish run" says what each failure means. 11. In a second pull request, set <version> on main to the next -SNAPSHOT (see above).

A tag is never moved or deleted. A mistake in a release is fixed by the next PATCH release, and the changelog says so. A version on Maven Central cannot be changed or removed once it is published.

docs.title: Maven Central
docs.text:
The artifact is ai.humem:tiervec. The namespace ai.humem is verified on the Central Portal (https://central.sonatype.com), account taewoon@humem.ai. Central accepts the artifact only with a complete pom.xml (name, description, url, license, developers, scm), a sources jar, a javadoc jar and a GnuPG signature on every file. The profile release in pom.xml builds and signs all of that, and the plugin central-publishing-maven-plugin uploads one bundle. The profile does not publish by default: the property central.autoPublish is false in pom.xml, so a local build and the dry run stop at VALIDATED or before. Only the publish run of the workflow passes -Dcentral.autoPublish=true -Dcentral.waitUntil=published, and then the Portal publishes the deployment as soon as it is valid. Creating the GitHub release is the deliberate act that starts it, and a published version cannot be taken back.

Only the workflow release-central.yml runs the profile with real credentials. Nobody runs it from a laptop.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
Four repository secrets of humemai/tiervec (Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions). The workflow reads nothing else.

Name What it holds CENTRAL_USERNAME The user name of the Central Portal user token CENTRAL_PASSWORD The password of the same token GPG_PRIVATE_KEY The armored private signing key GPG_PASSPHRASE The passphrase of that key

Check that the four names exist (the values cannot be read, and the command shows names only):

gh api repos/humemai/tiervec/actions/secrets --jq '[.secrets[].name]'

The workflow never prints a value, never puts one on a command line and never writes one to a file. The settings.xml it creates has ${env.CENTRAL_USERNAME} and ${env.CENTRAL_PASSWORD} references, mode 600, in the runner temp directory, and it removes the file and the GnuPG home at the end.

docs.title: The signing key
docs.text:
Create a key (a second key is not needed if one exists), store it as secrets without printing it, and publish the public key. <FPR> is the fingerprint that gpg --list-secret-keys --keyid-format long shows.

gpg --quick-generate-key "HumemAI tiervec releases <taewoon@humem.ai>" ed25519 sign 3y
gpg --list-secret-keys --keyid-format long taewoon@humem.ai

gpg --armor --export-secret-keys <FPR> | gh secret set GPG_PRIVATE_KEY --repo humemai/tiervec
gh secret set GPG_PASSPHRASE --repo humemai/tiervec

gpg --keyserver hkps://keyserver.ubuntu.com --send-keys <FPR>
gpg --armor --export <FPR> > tiervec-release-key.asc

gh secret set GPG_PASSPHRASE asks for the value, so it does not reach the shell history. Upload tiervec-release-key.asc at https://keys.openpgp.org/upload and follow the link in the e-mail it sends, then delete the file. Central looks the public key up on these key servers when it validates a signature, so a deployment fails validation until the key is published.

The token pair comes from the portal (Account, Generate User Token). Store it the same way, each command asks for its value:

gh secret set CENTRAL_USERNAME --repo humemai/tiervec
gh secret set CENTRAL_PASSWORD --repo humemai/tiervec

docs.title: Dry run
docs.text:
gh workflow run release-central.yml --ref <branch or main> -f dry-run=true
gh run list --workflow release-central.yml --limit 1
gh run view <run-id> --log-failed

The dry run is the default of the manual trigger and runs on any branch (GitHub dispatches a workflow only when its file is on main). It also runs on every pull request that changes pom.xml, src/main or the workflow file, so a Javadoc error or a broken release profile shows up in the pull request and not at release time; that check is not required. It generates a throwaway signing key inside the job, so it needs no secret and has no Central credentials: it cannot publish. It exports that key and imports it into a second GnuPG home with the script .github/scripts/import-signing-key.sh, the same script the publish run uses, so the import from an environment variable and the signing with a passphrase are rehearsed. It builds with JDK 21 (-Prelease -DskipTests, with a -SNAPSHOT version written as its release form in the job's checkout, because the Central plugin writes a bundle only for a release version), signs, writes the Central bundle, and then checks the bundle: the jar, sources jar, javadoc jar and pom are all there with checksums and a valid signature, the sources jar and the javadoc jar have content, and the pom has the elements Central requires. It uploads the bundle as the run artifact central-dry-run-bundle (7 days).

The dry run also checks and tests the scripts of the publish run: bash -n and shellcheck on every script in .github/scripts, and .github/scripts/test-central-scripts.sh. That test runs verify-central-release.sh and check-central-absent.sh against a local server that stands in for repo1.maven.org and the key server, throwaway signing keys and a Maven stub, so it needs nothing from the network. Each case spoils one thing (a flipped byte, a missing .asc, a wrong checksum, a bad signature, a signature of another key, a key that cannot be fetched, a jar that is not the built jar, a version that never appears) and the script must fail with the message of that thing; the good set must pass. To run it on a laptop: PYTHON_BIN="$(uv run --no-project python -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)')" bash .github/scripts/test-central-scripts.sh.

It does not prove that the real key, the passphrase and the token work, or that the key is on a key server. The publish run checks the first two early: it imports the key with the same script, signs a probe file with the passphrase, and stops before the build if that fails.

The dry run covers what changes with the code, such as a Javadoc error. Run it on the release branch before the tag (step 6).

docs.title: The publish run
docs.text:
The run starts when a GitHub release is published, or by hand with -f dry-run=false on the tag. Creating the release is the deliberate act: nothing else starts a publish. It refuses to run unless the ref is a tag that equals the version in pom.xml (a bare version, no -SNAPSHOT), the tagged commit is on main, the version is not on Maven Central yet, and all four secrets are present. "Not on Central yet" means that https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/ai/humem/tiervec/<version>/ answers 404, so a re-run cannot push a duplicate. An answer that is neither 404 nor 200 stops the run too, because "cannot tell" must not mean "go on".

What the run does, in order:

  1. Checks the tag, the pom version, that the commit is on main, that the version is not on Central, and the four secrets.
  2. Imports the signing key with .github/scripts/import-signing-key.sh and signs a probe file, so a wrong passphrase fails before the build. It keeps the fingerprint of the key (a public value) for step 6.
  3. Builds with the profile release and the fast tests, signs the jar, the sources jar, the javadoc jar and the pom, and uploads the bundle to the Central Portal. An expired Central token shows up here as an HTTP 401.
  4. The Portal validates the bundle and, because the run passes -Dcentral.autoPublish=true -Dcentral.waitUntil=published, publishes it. The Central plugin waits until the deployment is PUBLISHED, for at most central.waitMaxTime (3600 seconds).
  5. Waits for the sync from the Portal to repo1.maven.org: it polls https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/ai/humem/tiervec/<version>/tiervec-<version>.pom every 30 seconds, for at most 60 minutes, and fails with the last answer when the file never appears. (The search index of https://central.sonatype.com and search.maven.org is slower than the repository; the check uses repo1.maven.org only.)
  6. Verifies the result with .github/scripts/verify-central-release.sh: it downloads the jar, the sources jar, the javadoc jar and the pom with their .asc and checksum files; checks md5, sha1 and sha256 (and sha512 where served) against the bytes; fetches the public key from keyserver.ubuntu.com by the fingerprint of step 2 and checks that every signature is valid and made by that key; compares the three jars byte for byte with the jars that step 3 built, so what is on Central is what was built; and resolves ai.humem:tiervec:<version> with dependency:get in an empty local Maven repository with an isolated settings file (no mirrors, Central only).
  7. Writes the result in the job summary. The first version that passes also comments on issue #62 and closes it. A later version has no issue to comment on (releases are tracked by milestone, and a milestone or a GitHub release takes no comment), so the job summary and the run are its record.

To see it: gh run watch <run-id> --exit-status follows the run, and the job summary has the table of what Central serves. The Portal shows the deployment read-only at https://central.sonatype.com/publishing/deployments; there is nothing to press there.

What a failure means:

  • Red in step 3 with an HTTP 401: the Central token expired or is wrong. Rotate it (issue #97, the reminder below) and run the workflow again on the same tag.
  • Red in step 3 or 4 because the deployment is FAILED: nothing was published. Read the messages in the portal, drop the deployment, fix the cause, and run the workflow again on the same tag (gh workflow run release-central.yml --ref <version> -f dry-run=false). Fixing a problem in the sources needs a new version, because a tag is never moved.
  • Red in step 5 or 6: the version is published and is not taken back, whatever the verification said. If the pom never appeared within 60 minutes, run the workflow Verify on Maven Central (below) later. If a checksum, a signature or a jar differs, that is a real defect of the release: the fix is the next patch version, and its changelog says so.
  • A deployment that sits at VALIDATED (the run was stopped, or it was started with auto-publish set to false): press Publish for ai.humem:tiervec:<version> at https://central.sonatype.com/publishing/deployments, then run Verify on Maven Central. Do not run the publish run again while that deployment is in the portal: drop it first, because the check "not on Central yet" cannot see a deployment that is not synced.
  • To choose the manual path from the start, run the workflow by hand on the tag with -f dry-run=false -f auto-publish=false. It uploads, waits for VALIDATED and stops without publishing, the run summary says so, and the steps above for a deployment at VALIDATED apply. A release event always auto-publishes.

docs.title: Verify on Maven Central
docs.text:
The workflow Verify on Maven Central (verify-central.yml) runs the same verification for a version that is already out, with no secret and no write permission:

gh workflow run verify-central.yml -f version=<version> -f fingerprint=<FPR>

<FPR> is the 40 hex digits of the signing key: the line signing key fingerprint: in the log of the publish run, or gpg --list-keys --with-colons for the key on a laptop. It cannot compare the jars with a build, because it has none. Use it after a manual Publish, after a publish run that timed out while waiting, and to check an old version again.

docs.title: Reminder: the Central token expires
docs.text: The Central user token was created on 2026-11-12 with an expiry of one year, so it expires around 2027-11. Rotate it before then: generate a new token in the portal, set CENTRAL_USERNAME and CENTRAL_PASSWORD again, and keep the date of the new expiry here. An expired token shows as an authentication error (HTTP 401) in the upload step of the publish run, and the dry run cannot catch it because it uses no token. If the signing key has an expiry (the example above has three years), that date is a second rotation point: extend it with gpg --edit-key <FPR> expire, export it again as above and upload the public key again.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

The order of work follows one question: what does a database that embeds this index need from it? The list is ordered by that need. It has no dates. Each item is a GitHub issue with a problem statement, an acceptance test, and an explicit out-of-scope list. What exists today is in STATUS.md, and the architecture is in DESIGN.md.

docs.title: What a host needs
docs.text:
A host is the database that runs the index in its own process. These are the properties that decide whether an index fits a host, as opposed to fitting a benchmark:

  • A committed vector is found by the next query, exactly, also across a seal, a merge, or a swap.
  • Update and delete stay correct when the host reuses a record id.
  • A batch of adds and deletes becomes visible as a unit.
  • The index survives a crash and reopens without a full rebuild, and a damaged file is detected, never trusted.
  • A filter from the host's query language (an allowed set of ids) is fast and correct at every selectivity.
  • Memory is bounded, and the host, not the index, owns threads, build concurrency, and the memory budget.
  • Rebuild and merge cost does not stall queries while writes continue.
  • Small and medium collections work well by default, with few knobs.
  • It runs on the JVM and in a native image.

docs.title: Now
docs.text:
Decisions and tests that the rest of the work depends on.

  • #4: Choose the default merge policy: one large segment plus a small recent one
  • #5: Tests for record-id reuse and tombstone correctness across seal and merge
  • #6: Specify the segment file and the manifest
  • #7: Define the id epoch and the replay protocol for a host. Page: ID-EPOCH-AND-REPLAY.md. The epoch, the snapshot rebuild, and the replay in open are built, see STATUS.md.
  • #8: Document the host contract in docs/PROVIDER-CONTRACT.md. Page: PROVIDER-CONTRACT.md.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
Library work that follows from the items above. CI already runs the fast and the slow tests on JDK 21 and 25, so there is no separate item for that.

  • #9: Serialize sealed segments with a manifest, and reopen without a full rebuild. First cut: SEGMENT-FORMAT.md. Memory-mapped readers, non-empty tombstones, and lazy verification are not in it; they are tracked in #27. The host replays the tail through open with a record source (#7).
  • #10: Atomic apply(batch): adds and deletes become visible together. TieredIndex.apply and TieredIndex.awaitCapacity are built, see STATUS.md.
  • #11: Search context with a deadline and cancellation
  • #12: Allowed-id filters: measure the selectivity range and add fast paths
  • #13: Host-owned executor, build permits, and memory budget instead of own threads
  • #18: Configuration map, fingerprint, capability bits, and contract version
  • #14: Scalar twin of the graph kernel. Kern follows the same once-per-JVM switch as the flat kernels, so the graph and the tier also run without the Vector API module.
  • #15: Native-image build and smoke test in CI. The job native image smoke builds an image of the library with a small program that covers the flat, IVF, graph, and tiered indexes without the Vector API and compares every answer with an exact scan; the jobs native image smoke (vector, ...) do the same with the fp32 dot and squared L2 (#44) and the int8, SQ8, and block16 kernels (#48) on the Vector API. Segment files and concurrent writers are not in it.
  • #16: Merge by insertion into the largest segment
  • #17: Crash and corruption tests for the segment format

docs.title: Later
docs.text:
One tracking issue with a checklist: #19: Later: work that waits until the host contract holds

It covers 1-bit and 4-bit quantization schemes, IVF as a segment format, an on-disk graph, and other language bindings. Each item becomes its own issue when it is promoted.

docs.title: How to read measurements
docs.text: The harness is in the repository (BENCHMARKS.md), and no measurement is published yet. A single run (n=1) is descriptive: it shows what happened, not what usually happens. A claim of a 1.3x difference or larger needs at least five runs, each in a fresh JVM, and a smaller difference needs more. Every study states its claim, its arms, its number of runs, and the bound it must meet before it runs. Memory figures say which unit and which counter they use, and latency figures say whether the JIT was warm.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• A server. The index is a library that runs in the host's process, with no network between the host and the index.
  • A query language. The host parses SQL, Cypher, or anything else, and hands the index vectors and allowed-id sets.
  • Its own persistence of records. The host's records are the source of truth, and everything the index stores is derived and can be rebuilt from them.
  • GPU index builds or search.

docs.title: Segment files and the manifest
docs.text:
Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

This page describes what the code writes and reads today (the first cut of #9). A settled tier is written to a directory with TieredIndex.checkpoint(dir) and read back with TieredIndex.open(dir, config). One sealed graph can also be written alone with SealedGraph.serialize(file) and read with SealedGraph.load(file).

The records of the host stay the source of truth. Everything in the directory is derived data that can be deleted and rebuilt with TieredIndex.rebuildFrom. When open cannot trust the directory, it throws, and the host rebuilds from its records.

The claim the format makes: a process kill at any point of a publish leaves generation N or generation N+1 of the directory, plus files that the next open removes. No claim is made about power loss (see "What a crash leaves behind").

docs.title: Files in an index directory
docs.text:
File What it holds seg-<id>.tvs One immutable segment: the arrays of one SealedGraph. The id is zero-padded to at least six digits. tomb-<generation>.tvd The tombstone bitmaps of every segment of a generation. In this version they are all zero. manifest-<generation>.tvm One generation: the live segments, the tombstone file, a configuration fingerprint. The generation is zero-padded to 20 digits. *.tmp A file being written. Never named by a manifest. Removed at open.

Nothing that a manifest names is ever modified. A new state is a new manifest and, when needed, new segment files.

docs.title: Segment file
docs.text:
All numbers are little-endian. The file is, in order:

[0, 4096)                 header block
[4096, ...)               sections, each starting at a multiple of the alignment, in table order
[F, F + footer length)    footer: metadata and the section table
[end - 32, end)           locator

The header block holds nothing that depends on the section bytes, and the CRCs live in the footer, so a writer streams the file from front to back and never goes back.

docs.title: Header block
docs.text:
Offset Size Field 0 8 magic TVSEG001 8 2 major version 10 2 minor version 12 4 header length (52 in this version; the last 4 bytes of the header are its CRC) 16 4 byte-order probe 0x01020304 20 4 flags (none defined) 24 4 dim 28 4 stride_floats (equal to dim in this version; rows are not padded) 32 8 n, the number of rows 40 1 metric code: 0 cosine, 1 dot, 2 L2 41 1 id width in bytes (8) 42 1 layer 0 layout (0 is CSR, offsets plus edges) 43 1 reserved 44 4 section alignment (4096) 48 4 CRC32C of bytes 0 to 47 52 4044 zero fill, not covered by the CRC

Enums are stored as explicit codes, never as ordinals.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
Every section is a plain array of one fixed-width type. Each starts at a multiple of the alignment; the bytes between the end of one section and the start of the next are zero and are not covered by any CRC.

Id Name Element Count Notes 1 IDS i64 n Id of each row, in row order. Required. 2 VERS i64 n Version of each row, written by the tier. Optional for a standalone graph. 3 BYID i32 n Rows in increasing id order. A load uses it as is and does not sort. Required. 4 VEC f32 n * dim The fp32 vectors (unit length when the metric is cosine). Required. 5 LEVEL u8 n Top layer of each row. Required. 6 L0_OFF i32 n + 1 CSR offsets of layer 0. Required. 7 L0_EDGES i32 L0_OFF[n] Layer 0 neighbor rows. Required. 8 UP_IDX i32 n Index into UP_OFF for rows above layer 0, -1 otherwise. Required. 9 UP_OFF i32 free Offsets of the upper layers. Required. 10 UP_EDGES i32 free Neighbor rows of the upper layers. Required. 11 SQ8_CODES i8 n * dim Present when the graph has SQ8 codes. 12 SQ8_PARAMS f32 3 * n qbase, then qdelta, then qnorm. Present with section 11, never alone.

Section ids are never reused. The REQUIRED flag (bit 0 of the section flags) is set on the sections a reader cannot do without, and matters only for ids a reader does not know.

docs.title: Footer
docs.text:
The footer starts with 64 bytes of metadata, then one 40-byte entry per section.

Offset Size Field 0 4 entry row of the graph 4 4 top level 8 4 M 12 4 efConstruction 16 4 efSearch (a default for searches, not part of the data) 20 4 alpha (f32) 24 8 seed 32 8 smallest row version (0 when there is no VERS) 40 8 largest row version 48 4 flags: bit 0 is the SQ8 parameter flag 52 4 number of sections 56 4 offset of the first section entry (64 in this version) 60 4 reserved

A section entry is: id u16, flags u16, element width u32, element count u64, offset u64, length u64, CRC32C u32, reserved u32. The CRC covers exactly the section bytes.

docs.title: Locator
docs.text: The last 32 bytes: magic TVSEGEND (8), footer offset u64, footer length u32, footer CRC32C u32, total file length u64. The locator is the last thing written. A file that was cut short, or that has bytes appended, does not end in a locator that agrees with its own length, and fails after reading 32 bytes.

docs.title: Sizes
docs.text: The file holds the arrays of the in-memory graph, with VERS and BYID in place of the two sorted-id arrays the graph keeps, and no deletion bitmap. So, with VERS present, the sum of the section lengths equals SealedGraph.bytesHeld() minus 8 * ceil(n / 64) (the bitmap). The file length is 4096, plus the sections each rounded up to the alignment, plus 64 + 40 * sections, plus 32. SegmentFormatTest checks both for two dimensions, with and without SQ8.

docs.title: Integrity rules
docs.text:
• A reader reads the header block, the locator and the footer first, and checks the magic, the version, the byte-order probe, the header CRC, the locator against the real file length, and the footer CRC. This costs the same for a file of any size and happens before any section is read.
  • The section table is checked: offsets aligned, ascending, inside the file, element width times count equal to the length, the width and count of every known section as expected, all required sections present.
  • SegmentReader.read(file, true) also checks the CRC32C of every section and names the section that failed (CorruptException.section()). SealedGraph.load and TieredIndex.open always do. read(file, false) skips the section CRCs and is meant for inspection.
  • The stored id order is checked while it is used (rows in range, ids strictly increasing), and the layer 0 offsets are checked against the edge count.
  • A CRC32C detects accidental damage. It is not protection against tampering.

docs.title: Versioning and compatibility
docs.text:
A segment file has a format version major.minor.

  • A reader refuses a file with a larger major version (UnsupportedException).
  • A reader opens a file with a larger minor version. It ignores a section whose id it does not know, unless the section is marked required, in which case it refuses.
  • A newer minor may append header fields (the header length says where the header ends and where its CRC is) and footer metadata (the offset of the first section entry says where the table starts).
  • A different byte order, an id width other than 8, a layer 0 layout other than CSR, and a row stride other than dim are refused in this version.

The manifest and the tombstone file carry their own major.minor under the same rule. A manifest or a segment that an older reader does not understand is refused, not skipped: falling back to an older generation would silently serve stale data.

docs.title: Manifest and tombstone file
docs.text:
manifest-<generation>.tvm holds: magic TVMAN001, version, the body length, the generation, the epoch and the high-water id of the host (both "none" for a tier that never had an epoch; otherwise the host's epoch and the largest id that a segment holds), the version counter of the tier, the next free segment id, a fingerprint of the data-affecting configuration (dimension, metric, id width, M, efConstruction, whether SQ8 is on, the layer 0 layout), the generation, length and CRC of the tombstone file, one entry per live segment (id, row count, file length, the header CRC, smallest and largest row version), and a CRC32C of everything before it. File names are built from the ids in the manifest, never read from it.

tomb-<generation>.tvd holds: magic TVTOMB01, version, the generation, the number of segments, then for each segment its id, its row count and one bit per row, and a CRC32C. This version writes only zero bits and refuses a file with a bit set.

docs.title: Publish
docs.text:
Manifest.publish makes a new generation live. The segment files it names are written and flushed first (SegmentWriter.write creates a new file and flushes it).

Step Action Hook point (FaultHook.Step) 1, 2 Write the segment files, flush each SEGMENTS_WRITTEN 3 Write and flush the tombstone file, flush the directory DIR_SYNCED_AFTER_SEGMENTS 4 Write the manifest under a temporary name MANIFEST_TMP_WRITTEN 5 Flush the temporary manifest MANIFEST_TMP_SYNCED 6 Rename it to manifest-<generation>.tvm MANIFEST_RENAMED 7 Flush the directory DIR_SYNCED_AFTER_RENAME 8 The caller switches its in-memory view, then Manifest.gc deletes what the new manifest does not name (none)

The rename is the only moment a generation becomes visible, and by then every byte it names was already flushed. Generation N is deleted only in step 8, after step 7, so an unfinished N+1 can exist only while N and all its files still exist. A manifest is never overwritten: publishing a generation that exists is an error.

On Windows the directory flush of steps 3 and 7 does nothing, because Java cannot open a directory there (FileChannel.open is refused). File contents are still forced with FileChannel.force, so the bytes of every file are flushed before the rename. The directory entry (the new name, the rename) is not flushed by the library, so a power loss right after a rename can lose the rename on Windows. A process kill is covered on Windows as on Linux, because the claim above is about process kills only.

docs.title: What a crash leaves behind
docs.text:
The table is for a process kill (the page cache survives). A crash after a step leaves:

Crash after Visible generation Left on disk for the next open to remove 1 or 2 N a complete or partial new segment file 3 N new segment files and the new tombstone file 4 or 5 N and a temporary manifest 6 or 7 N+1 the files of generation N 8 N+1 whatever the cleanup had not yet deleted

ManifestCrashTest and TierReopenTest run the publish with a hook that throws after each step and check which generation readLatest and open find, that the segments serve the same results as the in-memory graphs, and that the next open leaves exactly the files of that generation. This covers a process kill only. It does not check that the flushes are issued in the right order, and it says nothing about power loss: that needs a simulated file system that discards data that was not flushed, which this version does not have.

docs.title: Open
docs.text:
TieredIndex.open(dir, config):

  1. Manifest.readLatest: list the manifests, newest first. For each, check magic, version, CRC, that every named file exists with the recorded length and a valid header, footer and locator, and that the tombstone file matches. The first that passes is current. A candidate that fails is skipped. If none passes it throws CorruptException; an empty directory throws NoSuchFileException; a manifest in a newer format throws UnsupportedException at once.
  2. Compare the fingerprint with the configuration (dimension, metric, M, efConstruction, SQ8). A difference throws MismatchException.
  3. Read every segment with every section checksummed, and compare it with its manifest entry.
  4. Delete the files that the manifest does not name (orphans of a crashed publish, older generations).
  5. Restore the version counter and the epoch, and start the tier with the segments, an empty tail and an empty floor map.

Any failure throws. The overload open(dir, dim, metric, config, rebuildSource) catches it and builds the tier from the records with rebuildFrom; openFallbackCause() tells why. The directory is left as it was in that case, and the next checkpoint replaces its contents.

open(dir, dim, metric, config, recordSource) adds, after step 5, the epoch comparison (another epoch gives a cold index), the drop of ids above the host's recovered maximum (rebuilt segments and a new generation before it returns), the liveness check, and the replay of the host's live records above the high-water id: see ID-EPOCH-AND-REPLAY.md.

docs.title: What the first cut leaves out
docs.text:
• Memory mapping. A segment is read into the heap arrays of SealedGraph.
  • Replay of the tail by the library itself. The host replays what the segments lack through RecordSource.
  • Tombstones. checkpoint refuses a tier with a non-empty tail, a non-empty floor map, or a segment with hidden copies (an IllegalStateException), and SegmentWriter refuses a graph with soft-deleted rows. The tombstone file exists and is verified, but holds only zeros. Rebuilding the floor map from bitmaps is the follow-up.
  • Lazy and chunked CRC verification. Every section is verified at open.
  • The fixed-stride layer 0 layout and padded rows.
  • Formats for the flat tail and for IVF.
  • A lock file and a marker for an unclean shutdown. One process must own a directory.
  • A simulated file system for power loss tests.
  • Per-segment repair: any integrity failure rebuilds the whole tier.

docs.title: Record-id reuse and tombstones
docs.text:
A host database frees a record id and later gives it to a new record, so the tier sees delete(id) followed by add(id, newVector). The version floor of TieredIndex keeps the old copies of an id hidden while the new vector is visible. Tests cover this (#5). They use a model that holds the current vector of every id and keeps the older vectors, so a resurrected vector is recognised by its score.

Cases, each on a fresh index:

Case What it does a_tail The old copy sits in the active tail: delete 30 percent, re-add 80 percent of them with new vectors, delete and re-add again, then seal a2_tail_and_segments The old copies sit in one segment and in the tail: delete, re-add, seal, merge b_sealed The old copies sit in sealed segments: delete, re-add (the new vector in the tail, the old one below the floor), seal beside the old copies, delete and re-add again, seal, merge c1_reuse_in_merge Re-add, and delete then re-add, inside a running merge of the segments that hold the old copies; then again after the merge c2_delete_in_merge Delete, delete then re-add, delete then re-add then delete, replace, and brand-new ids, all inside a running merge; no delete may be lost when the merged segment is swapped in e_floor_chain One set of ids goes through four generations, each in its own segment, so the floor moves up four times; then a merge s_seal_window Operations inside the publish window of a seal, with the frozen tail holding every old copy (before the swap) and right after the swap, using setSealHooks f_fuzz_background Slow variant only: the background worker seals and merges while one writer reuses, replaces and deletes ids and one reader searches all the time; a hit counts only for an id that was untouched for the whole search

Every checkpoint searches plain, with the id alone allowed, and under Freshness.SEALED_ONLY, with the current vector and with an older vector of the id as the query. A deleted id, an older vector's score, a repeated id, a wrong score, or a reused id at rank 1 for its old vector fails the run. size() and stats().live() are compared with the model, and the floor map must be empty after a full merge in the deterministic cases. A merge window or seal window that is not reached fails the run, it is never skipped.

The tests are RidReuseTest (fast: n = 3000, dimension 32 and 128, two seeds, all deterministic cases, no reader thread), RidReuseLongTest and RidReuseBigLongTest (slow: all cases including the background case, with a concurrent reader that counts a hit only for an id untouched while the search ran; n = 3000 with three seeds on three configurations, and n = 20000), RidReuseSwapRaceTest (fast, about one second: a search paused inside its allow predicate while mergeNow() swaps and cleans up the floor), RebuildSwapRaceTest (fast: two searches paused inside their allow predicate while rebuildFrom swaps the rebuilt state in), and RidReuseMutantTest and RidReuseMutantLongTest. The probe itself is RidReuseProbe.

The probe found a race between a search and a merge swap (#26): a search that started before the swap could return an id that was deleted before it started, or an older vector of an id that was deleted and added again, because the merge removed the floor entries that the old segments still needed. The fix: a search counts itself on the view it reads, a view that a swap replaces while searches run on it is held, and the floor entries that a segment of a held view needs stay until those searches are done (the worker, awaitIdle, mergeNow, sealNow and checkpoint drop them then). The query path still takes no lock and starts no thread: it does one atomic add and one atomic subtract per search. RidReuseSwapRaceTest holds a search inside the first call of its filter, runs mergeNow(), lets the search go on, and checks the answer and that the entry is dropped afterwards; it failed on the code before the fix.

rebuildFrom had the same race on the recovery path (#28): it cleared the floor map before it swapped the rebuilt view in, so a search that was running on the old view could see a hidden copy as valid. It now swaps through the same publish call as a merge and settles the floor the same way, so the entries stay until the searches of the old view are done. RebuildSwapRaceTest holds one search with the vector of a deleted id and one with the older vector of an id that was added again, runs rebuildFrom with the live records, lets both go on, and checks the answers and that the floor map is empty after awaitIdle.

A probe that cannot fail is not a test, so the mutant tests check that it fails on a broken tier. The test reads TieredIndex.java, applies one single-line change (the anchor must occur exactly once), compiles the copy with the JDK compiler API into a temporary directory, and runs the probe in a class loader that prefers that directory. TieredIndex.java itself has no test hook. This needs a JDK, not a JRE: without a compiler the mutant tests are skipped with a message, and they fail when the CI environment variable is set.

Mutant Change The probe must report X0 none (control) a clean run M1 add removes the floor entry of the id instead of raising it staleHits above 0, in b_sealed M2 delete takes a version but writes no floor entry lostDeletes above 0, in b_sealed M3 cleanupFloor drops every entry after a merge a wrong answer in c2_delete_in_merge

docs.title: Id epoch and replay
docs.text:
The host names its numbering of ids with an epoch (#7, ID-EPOCH-AND-REPLAY.md). rebuildFrom(Supplier<Snapshot>, long) rebuilds from the host's snapshot without the write lock: the library records the writes that arrive during the build and applies them after the swap, adds at or below the snapshot position skipped. checkpoint stores the epoch and the high-water id (the largest id a segment holds) in the manifest, which already had the two fields, so the format version is the same. open(dir, dim, metric, config, RecordSource) discards persisted state of another epoch (a cold index), drops held ids above the id the host recovered and makes that durable before it returns, hides ids that the host no longer holds, and adds the host's live records above the high-water id to the tail.

The tests use FakeHost, a host that holds the records, mints increasing ids, and forgets its unflushed transactions in a simulated crash: EpochReplayTest (deterministic, fast), EpochReplayStressTest (a crash and reopen loop with random fault points, and a host thread that writes while the tier is rebuilt; three seeds, fast), and EpochReplayLongTest (the same, longer, slow). Not covered: power loss, a crash inside the replay itself, a crash inside the publish that open makes when it drops rows, a check of the id order, and a delete that the library persisted and the host then forgot (the host flushes its deletes before it lets the library checkpoint).

docs.title: Atomic batches
docs.text:
TieredIndex.apply(batch) applies the adds and then the deletes of one host transaction under one hold of the write lock, and a search sees all of the batch or none of it (#10). Applying the same batch again changes nothing visible. awaitCapacity(deadlineNanos) is the separate back pressure check: apply never waits for the worker and does not look at the hard tail limit, so one batch can take the tail above it.

The tail and the floor map change in place, so one volatile write of a new view cannot cover a batch. A batch counter does: it is odd while a batch is applied and even otherwise. A search waits while it is odd and reads it again after its scan, and when it changed, the scan is thrown away and run again. The query path still takes no lock and creates no thread: one volatile read before the scan, one fence and one read after it. A search that meets a batch waits for it (the length of one batch), and a stream of batches that follow each other faster than one scan takes can starve a search.

The tests are ApplyBatchTest (fast) and ApplyStressTest (slow). ApplyBatchTest checks that the whole batch is visible after apply returns, that a batch with a bad vector changes nothing, that applying a batch again changes nothing visible (also after a seal), that a search held inside its first allow call while a batch is applied answers from the state before the batch or the state after it and never from a mixture (once with the old id in the tail and once with the old id in a segment), that apply does not wait for a worker that is inside a seal, and the behavior of awaitCapacity at the hard tail limit. ApplyStressTest runs updater threads that move groups of ids from one generation to the next in batches while searcher threads check that a group always shows exactly its ids of one generation, on a tail and on a tier that seals and merges all the time.

docs.title: Graph self-search recall
docs.text:
The graph index is approximate, so a search for a vector that is equal to an inserted one can miss it (#38). Measured at the default ef (100): at 100,000 to 200,000 vectors the graph index misses a query equal to an inserted vector at about 1.2e-4 to 4.0e-4 per probe (1,600,000 probes in each of four modes, 188 to 636 misses per mode). Every one of the 1,260 misses that were diagnosed was reachable from the entry point on layer 0, and a search at ef 1000 found 1,254 of them. At the size of the threaded program (below 67,000 vectors) there was 1 miss in 112 runs of 3,360 probes. These are measurements of the default ef, not a guarantee, and the rate rises with the size of the index.

The threaded program (GraphConcurrencyTest) therefore checks read-your-writes in two parts. Exact membership: right after add returned, the id must be in the index, with no tolerance. It is read through the id-to-ordinal map and the node state (GraphIndex.containsForTest, a package-private accessor for tests), not through a search. Self-search: a recall check that searches for the vector just inserted at ten times the default ef (1000) and fails on more than 1 miss per run (3,360 probes in the 60 s program). Each run prints one line, RYW membership checks=N missing=0 selfSearchMisses=K of M. GraphReadYourWritesTest (fast) covers both parts on 3,000 vectors with a tolerance of 0, and checks that the probe reports an id that is not in the index.

docs.title: What does not exist yet
docs.text:
• Serialization of IVF and of the flat tail. FlatIndex has its own serialize and load. The graph segments and a settled tier have the first cut (SEGMENT-FORMAT.md): copy-based reads, no memory mapping, no tail replay, no non-empty tombstones (checkpoint refuses a tier with a tail, a floor entry, or hidden copies), every section verified at open. When open fails, the host falls back to rebuildFrom.
  • Engine integration. Nothing here is wired into ArcadeDB or any other engine.
  • IVF as a segment type of the tier. IvfIndex is standalone.
  • Native-image coverage beyond the smoke job. The program does not write or read segment files (checkpoint, open), does not call rebuildFrom, and uses no concurrent writers; the image is built on Linux (x86-64 and arm64) and on macOS arm64 in CI, and on Windows x64 in the vector job only (there is no scalar image job on Windows), and it is not published.
  • A stable API. 0.1.0 is the first release. Until 1.0 a breaking change to the supported surface needs a new minor version (API.md). The version rule, the steps and the Maven Central details are in RELEASING.md.
  • Published measurements. The experiment's own measurements are in a private harness. The harness Bench (BENCHMARKS.md) is in the repository and the CI job bench smoke runs it at 10,000 vectors, but no result file is committed yet.
  • The longer mode of the graph test program (a recall curve at n = 20000) is not wired into the JUnit tests.

docs.text:
• The Java package is ai.humem.tiervec, the name of the library. It was renamed from the package of the first import before the first release, so it is not a breaking change. The system property that forces the scalar twins is ai.humem.tiervec.scalar.
  • Comments and Javadoc in the sources were rewritten in plain words: the experiment-internal names (requirement ids, fix numbers, rule names) are gone, and no code changed in that edit.

  • The micro-benchmark FlatMicro and the benchmark harness of the experiment are not part of this repository. Bench and NativeSmoke are new programs written for it, not imports.
  • One edit to a main source, GraphIndex.java (issue #3, found by the slow CI job): consolidate(), repairOrphans and seal() size their bitsets and arrays from a snapshot of nextOrd, and a concurrent add can publish a node allocated after the snapshot as the entry point (or, in repairOrphans, return one from its search), so the node index fell past the end. bit now reads an index past the end as not set, repairOrphans sizes its arrays to cover the entry point, and seal() ignores an entry point from after its snapshot. GraphConsolidateRaceTest builds that view without threads. It was pushed alone first and failed the fast job on the unfixed code.

docs.title: tiervec
docs.text:
Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

A tiered vector index for agent-memory databases on the JVM.

Status: experimental. The API is not stable, the first release is 0.1.0, and nothing is wired into a database engine yet. No benchmark numbers are published. What is proven says what the repository shows today, and docs/STATUS.md has the detail.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A library of vector-index algorithms meant to live inside a database engine, in the same process, with no network between the engine and the index. The first host is ArcadeDB.

The design follows the workload of an agent's memory: many small and medium collections, a steady stream of small writes, deletes and updates, and queries that must see a write right away.

  • Exact tail. Recent writes sit in a bounded buffer that is scanned exactly, so a write is visible to the next query without waiting for an index build.
  • Sealed segments. Older vectors live in immutable HNSW graph segments. Below a size threshold no graph is built and every search is an exact scan. Segments are merged in the background and swapped in atomically.
  • Tombstones with a version floor handle deletes and updates, including ids that a database reuses after a delete.
  • Scalar twins of every kernel (flat, IVF, and graph), chosen once per JVM, so every index, the graph tier and the tiered index included, also runs without the Vector API module.
  • Pure Java, no native dependencies. It also builds into a GraalVM native image, where every kernel except hamming (fp32, int8, SQ8, and block) uses the Vector API too (see Native image).

The repository also holds a standalone IVF (inverted file) index, which is not a tier segment yet. The host engine would own persistence, transactions and recovery: the tier can rebuild all of its derived state from the raw vectors. Serialization exists for the flat index and, as a first cut, for a settled tier: segment files with a manifest, written by TieredIndex.checkpoint and read by TieredIndex.open (docs/SEGMENT-FORMAT.md). docs/DESIGN.md describes what the code does.

docs.text:
Every row says what the repository itself shows, and links the evidence. "Not measured yet" means no number is published here.

Question Where it stands Evidence Does it build and pass its tests? Yes, on Linux x86-64 (JDK 21 and 25, fast and slow tests), Linux arm64, macOS arm64 and Windows x64 (fast tests only on these three). Native image smoke jobs run on the same four platforms. Platform support, docs/STATUS.md Sizes the tests use The tests run on small collections. The long id-reuse test (RidReuseBigLongTest) and the long IVF program use 20,000 vectors, and the threaded graph program stays below 67,000. A self-search probe on the graph index ran at 100,000 to 200,000 vectors. docs/STATUS.md Speed and recall at scale Not measured yet. No benchmark numbers are published in this repository, and nothing here is proven at 1,000,000 vectors or at 10,000,000. A harness for these measurements exists, and CI runs it at 10,000 vectors as a smoke test. docs/BENCHMARKS.md, docs/STATUS.md Concurrent readers and writers Tested at small sizes: threaded programs of 5 to 60 seconds, batch stress tests, and tests that hold a search inside a merge or a seal. Concurrent writers at scale: not proven. docs/STATUS.md Deletes, updates, reused ids, atomic batches Tested, including races between a search and a merge or a rebuild. The races found so far (#3, #26, #28) have tests. docs/STATUS.md, docs/STATUS.md Restart and recovery A settled tier can be checkpointed and reopened. Tests stop the publish after each step (a simulated process kill), flip bits in every byte that a CRC covers, and forge files with valid CRCs. Power loss is not tested. docs/SEGMENT-FORMAT.md, docs/STATUS.md Native image Smoke tests build and run an image and compare every answer with an exact scan. They do not cover segment files, rebuildFrom or concurrent writers. The image is not published. docs/STATUS.md Inside a database engine No. Nothing here is wired into ArcadeDB or any other engine. docs/PROVIDER-CONTRACT.md Release 0.1.0 is the first release. The Maven coordinates are ai.humem:tiervec. The API is not stable. CHANGELOG.md, docs/RELEASING.md

Known limits

  • Graph search is approximate. At the default ef (100), a query equal to an inserted vector is missed at about 1.2e-4 to 4.0e-4 per probe at 100,000 to 200,000 vectors, and the rate rises with the size of the index. A search at ef 1000 found 1,254 of the 1,260 misses that were diagnosed. The hardware of this measurement is not recorded. (details)
  • A filtered search with a small allowed share (about 0.01) spends most of its cost on a walk that falls back to an exact scan. The opt-in filterScanBelow skips the walk, it is off by default, and the range of shares where it pays is not measured yet (#12, docs/DESIGN.md).
  • checkpoint writes a settled tier only: no tail, no tombstones. Reads copy the file into memory, with no memory mapping (docs/SEGMENT-FORMAT.md).
  • A search that meets a batch waits for it, and a stream of batches that follow each other faster than one scan takes can starve a search (docs/STATUS.md).
  • In a native image a result can differ from the JVM by rounding. AVX-512 and SVE are not used (#52).

docs.text:
mvn -B -ntp verify            # fast tests: Vector API kernels, then the scalar twins
mvn -B -ntp verify -Pslow     # the long concurrency and stress tests (tag "slow")

The tests are test programs, wrapped as JUnit 5 tests. A wrapper runs the program, asserts that no check failed, and asserts that at least the expected number of checks ran. The benchmark harness is not part of the Maven build: docs/BENCHMARKS.md says how to compile and run it.

docs.title: Native image
docs.text:
The library runs in a GraalVM native image. The CI job native image smoke builds the scalar image, and the jobs native image smoke (vector, ...) build the vector image on x86-64 and arm64 Linux and on macOS arm64 (GraalVM Community 25.0.2). The scalar image also builds on arm64 Linux (native image smoke (arm64 Linux)) and on macOS arm64 (native image smoke (macOS arm64)). The job native image smoke (vector, Windows x64) builds the vector image on Windows x64; there is no scalar image job on Windows.

  • In an image every kernel that has a Vector API form uses it through NKernels (flat, IVF, and graph): the fp32 dot and l2sq, the int8 dot, the SQ8 dots, and block16. The species is fixed when the image is built: 256 bits on x86-64, 128 bits on aarch64 (where the Vector API has no 32-bit byte species, so the byte kernels load 64 or 128 bits of bytes and split them into parts). The Vector API kernels of the JVM are more than 10 times slower than scalar code in an image, so the image does not use them; NKernels is the form that the image compiles to SIMD code.
  • hamming has no Vector API form and stays scalar, in an image and on a JVM. AVX-512 and SVE are not used (the species stay 256 and 128 bits until measured).
  • A result in an image can differ from a result on a JVM by rounding, because the lane sum of NKernels has the order of the instruction. Results are still bitwise equal between two calls on equal data within one image.
  • To build an image with the Vector API kernels, give the image builder --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector -H:+VectorAPISupport. The jar carries META-INF/native-image/ai.humem/tiervec/native-image.properties, which sets --initialize-at-build-time=ai.humem.tiervec.NKernels for an application that has the jar on its class path; the species must be fixed at build time, or the kernels are slow. -H:+VectorAPISupport is an experimental option of GraalVM 25, and it needs GraalVM 25 or newer.
  • Without --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector the image has the scalar twins for every kernel. -Dai.humem.tiervec.scalar=true forces the scalar twins in an image as well, when the property is set before the library is first used (an image takes -D options on its command line).
  • The smoke program prints informational SPEED lines, one per kernel (dot, dotI8, dotF8, dotF8x4, and block16 per block of 16 vectors), with the median time of 1,000,000 calls on 768 dimensions next to the scalar twin. They are not a bar.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• JDK 21 or newer. CI builds and tests with Temurin 21 and 25 on x86-64 Linux, and runs the fast tests on arm64 Linux (JDK 21 and 25) and arm64 macOS (JDK 21). The job fast tests (Windows x64, JDK 21) runs the fast tests on Windows x64 (not the slow tests).
  • Maven 3.9 or newer.
  • The Vector API is an incubator module in these JDKs. Compile with --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector, and run with it to get the Vector API kernels; the pom.xml sets it for the compiler and for the test JVMs. At run time the module is optional: every kernel (flat, IVF, and graph) falls back to its scalar twin when the module is missing, or when -Dai.humem.tiervec.scalar=true is set.
  • On a JVM with the Vector API, x86-64 vectorizes the fp32 dot and l2sq, the int8 dot, the SQ8 dots, and block16. On aarch64 (NEON, 128-bit float lanes) the fp32 dot and l2sq use the JVM kernels and the int8 dot, the SQ8 dots, and block16 use the 128-bit forms of NKernels. hamming is scalar everywhere. A JVM with 128-bit lanes that is not aarch64 runs those four as scalar code. AVX-512 and SVE are not used (#52).
  • Nothing else at run time. JUnit 5 is a test dependency.

Tier 2: measured. None yet. No benchmark numbers are published in this repository. The harness is described in docs/BENCHMARKS.md; a row moves here when a result file with its hardware, JDK and commit is committed under results/. The SPEED lines that the native image jobs print are informational, and the one measurement in the repository (the graph self-search recall in docs/STATUS.md) does not record its hardware. The shared GitHub runners are not a benchmark machine: a timing from them is a ratio between two things measured in the same run, not an absolute speed. A row moves here when its numbers and its hardware are published.

Tier 3: best effort. The code is plain Java 21 and has no native dependency, so it is expected to work, but nothing checks it and a problem there is fixed when it is cheap to do.

  • macOS on Intel (x86-64): no CI job.
  • Other JDK vendors and other JDK versions than 21 and 25: only Temurin 21 and 25 are tested.
  • Other Linux distributions and other CPU features: the CI runners fix them. AVX-512 and SVE are not used (#52).

Out: Windows on ARM, until GraalVM and the libraries around it support it. Nothing here builds or tests it.

docs.text:
The pages below are published at https://docs.humem.ai/tiervec/. The default version is latest, the newest release (0.1.0). The version dev follows main and has changes that are not released yet. The site is built from the Markdown files of this repository (how to build it).

  • docs/API.md: the supported public classes, the internal ones, and what may change in a 0.x release.
  • docs/DESIGN.md: the architecture and the knobs of the tier configuration.

  • docs/SEGMENT-FORMAT.md: the segment file, the manifest, the publish order, and reopen, as the first cut implements them.
  • docs/BENCHMARKS.md: the benchmark harness, how to run it, and what a result file holds.

All notable changes to tiervec are in this file. The layout follows Keep a Changelog. The version rule and the steps of a release are in docs/RELEASING.md. Until 1.0, a breaking change to the supported surface (docs/API.md) needs a new minor version.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • Creating the GitHub release now publishes to Maven Central by itself and verifies the result (checksums, signatures, the built jars, a resolution from a fresh local repository), so the Publish click in the Central Portal is gone (docs/RELEASING.md).

The first release. It is the sources of the first experiment, imported and brought to the supported surface in docs/API.md. Nothing was released under the old package name. Details are in docs/STATUS.md.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• FlatIndex: exact scan with optional SQ8 or binary codes, compaction, serialize and load.
  • GraphIndex: a concurrent HNSW graph with delete, consolidate, and optional SQ8.
  • IvfIndex: a standalone inverted-file index with lazy training, background retrain and drift detection.
  • TieredIndex: an exact tail, sealed graph segments, background merges, tombstones with a version floor, atomic batches (apply, awaitCapacity), rebuildFrom, and an opt-in scan-first plan for filtered searches (filterScanBelow).
  • Persistence of a settled tier: TieredIndex.checkpoint and TieredIndex.open, with segment files and a manifest (docs/SEGMENT-FORMAT.md), and RecordSource for reconciling a reopened tier with the records of a host database (docs/ID-EPOCH-AND-REPLAY.md).
  • Scalar twins of every kernel, used when the Vector API module is missing, and Vector API kernels for aarch64 and for GraalVM native images.
  • A GraalVM native image smoke test on Linux (x86-64 and arm64), macOS arm64 and Windows x64.
  • CI on JDK 21 and 25, with the fast tests also on arm64 and on Windows x64.
  • Community files (CONTRIBUTING, SECURITY, SUPPORT, and the issue and pull request templates) and the platform support table in the README.
  • The supported public surface and the stability policy (docs/API.md).
  • A benchmark harness for the tier (src/bench, docs/BENCHMARKS.md) with a CI smoke at 10,000 vectors. No result file is published yet.
  • Maven Central publishing for ai.humem:tiervec: the metadata Central requires in pom.xml, a release profile (sources jar, javadoc jar, GnuPG signatures, upload to the Central Portal), and the workflow release-central.yml with a dry run (docs/RELEASING.md).
  • The documentation is published as a release version with the alias latest when a version tag is pushed, and dev stays the label of main.

docs.title: Contributing to tiervec

tiervec is a Java library of vector-index algorithms that is meant to run inside a database engine. It is experimental: the first release is 0.1.0 and the API is not stable yet (see docs/STATUS.md). Small, focused contributions are welcome.

tiervec is licensed under the Apache License 2.0. When you submit a contribution, you agree that it is licensed under the same terms (Section 5 of the licence). You keep your copyright. There is no separate contributor agreement.

Do not copy code or text into the repository unless its licence is compatible with Apache 2.0. Papers and libraries that the work builds on are listed in THIRD_PARTY.md. The library has no run-time dependencies, and a new one needs a strong reason.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A security problem is not an issue. Follow SECURITY.md.
  • A question is not a bug. See SUPPORT.md.
  • Search the open issues first. If your idea is not there, open an issue and say what problem it solves. For a new feature or a change in behavior, wait for an answer before you write much code.
  • Read docs/DESIGN.md and docs/PROVIDER-CONTRACT.md. They say what the library does and what it promises to a host database.

docs.title: Build and test
docs.text:
You need JDK 21 or newer and Maven 3.9 or newer.

mvn -B -ntp verify            # fast tests: Vector API kernels, then the scalar twins
mvn -B -ntp verify -Pslow     # the long concurrency and stress tests (tag "slow")

The fast tests run on every pull request, on JDK 21 and 25. The slow tests also run on every pull request, on x86-64 Linux, and take about 45 minutes. You do not have to run them on your own machine.

docs.title: Build the documentation
docs.text:
The site at https://docs.humem.ai/tiervec/dev/ is built with MkDocs Material from the README, the other Markdown files in the repository root, and docs/. The hook docs-site/hooks.py turns the root files into pages and rewrites relative links: a link to another page stays a link to that page, and a link to any other file in the repository becomes a link to it on GitHub. The design system in docs/brand is a vendored copy. Do not edit it: change it in humemai/design-system and vendor it again. bash docs/brand/verify.sh checks the copy. To build the site as the check does:

uv run --no-project --python 3.12 --with-requirements docs-site/requirements.txt mkdocs build --strict

The build fails on a link that points nowhere. The workflow deploy-docs.yml publishes the site as dev when a change to the docs reaches main.

docs.title: Make a change
docs.text:
1. Fork the repository and branch from main.
  2. Keep the change small. One pull request does one thing.
  3. Add a test. A test for a bug fix must fail on the old code and pass on the new. Say in the pull request how you checked that.
  4. Run the fast tests. A change in a kernel must keep the scalar twin and the Vector API form in agreement (see KernDiffTest).
  5. Update the documentation that your change makes wrong: the README, the files in docs/, and the Javadoc.
  6. Open a pull request. Say what changed and why, and write Closes #N for the issue it fixes.

Commit messages start with the area, then a short summary and the issue number, for example Tests: replace absolute throughput floors in concurrency tests with an overlap proof (#59).

Pull requests are squash-merged into main, so the history is linear.

docs.title: Checks that must pass
docs.text:
Three checks are required before a merge:

  • fast tests (JDK 21)
  • fast tests (JDK 25)
  • Ensure SHA pinned actions

The other jobs (arm64, Windows, native image, slow tests, the documentation build) also run on a pull request. A failure there is read like any other failure, even where the check is not required.

docs.title: Workflow files
docs.text: Every action in .github/workflows/ is pinned to a full commit SHA, with the version as a comment. A floating tag fails the check Ensure SHA pinned actions.

docs.title: Measurements
docs.text: Do not put a performance number in a pull request or in the documentation unless you can say how it was measured: the hardware, the JDK, the data, the number of runs. Timing numbers from the shared GitHub runners are useful as ratios between two things measured in the same run. They are not absolute speed.

docs.title: Conduct
docs.text: Be polite and be specific. Disagree with the code or the idea, not with the person. Harassment is not tolerated, and the maintainer may remove comments and block people who harass others.

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text:
Do not open a public issue for a security problem.

Use GitHub's private reporting: open the Security tab of the repository and choose Report a vulnerability. Or send an email to info@humem.ai with the subject tiervec security. Either way a maintainer reads it, replies, and works with you on a fix before anything is made public.

Please include:

  • The version or the commit of tiervec.
  • The JDK (the output of java -version), the operating system and the CPU architecture.
  • Whether the Vector API module is on (--add-modules jdk.incubator.vector), or the scalar twins are in use, or the code runs in a native image.
  • A description of the problem and its impact.
  • Steps to reproduce it, or a small program that shows it.

docs.title: What counts
docs.text:
tiervec is a library that runs in the process of its host. It opens no socket and reads no file that the host did not point it to. These are in scope:

  • A file in a segment directory that makes TieredIndex.open or SegmentReader read or write memory outside the file, loop without end, or allocate without a bound, other than by throwing an exception. The format checks its sections with CRC32C, but a CRC detects accidental damage and is no protection against tampering (see docs/SEGMENT-FORMAT.md), so a hostile file must still not do harm.
  • A search that returns a vector for an id that was deleted, or that returns data from another index.
  • A flaw in the build or in the workflow files that lets an outside party run code in CI or change a release.

A wrong answer, a crash on bad input that ends in an exception, and a slow query are ordinary bugs. Open an issue for them.

docs.text: The first release is 0.1.0. A fix goes to the latest minor version as a new patch version, and main gets it too (see the version rule in docs/RELEASING.md).

docs.text: tiervec is a small open source project with one maintainer and no fixed response time. You get a reply, and credit in the fix if you want it. No bounty is paid.
